knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical real QCQP allowing affine and constant terms in every quadratic function.

source_refs.locator: 3.9 The GOP for Quadratically Constrained Problems p. 96

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
An inhomogeneous quadratically constrained quadratic program has the form
\[\operatorname*{minimize}_{x\in\mathbb R^n}\quad q_0(x):=x^{\mathsf T}Q_0x+2c_0^{\mathsf T}x+d_0\]
subject to \(q_i(x):=x^{\mathsf T}Q_ix+2c_i^{\mathsf T}x+d_i\le 0\) for every \(i\in I\) and \(q_j(x):=x^{\mathsf T}Q_jx+2c_j^{\mathsf T}x+d_j=0\) for every \(j\in E\), where \(I\) and \(E\) are finite disjoint index sets. For every objective or constraint index \(k\), \(Q_k\in\mathbb S^n\), \(c_k\in\mathbb R^n\), and \(d_k\in\mathbb R\). The adjective inhomogeneous means that linear or constant terms may be nonzero; no definiteness assumption is imposed unless separately stated.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An inhomogeneous QCQP minimizes a quadratic polynomial subject to separately indexed quadratic equalities and inequalities, with linear and constant terms permitted in the objective and constraints.
knowledge_statements.title: Inhomogeneous QCQP

source_witnesses.locator: 3.9 The GOP for Quadratically Constrained Problems p. 96

knowledge_statements.title: Homogeneous QCQP
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical real homogeneous formulation, containing only quadratic forms.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A homogeneous quadratically constrained quadratic program has the form
\[\operatorname*{minimize}_{x\in\mathbb R^n}\quad x^{\mathsf T}Q_0x\]
subject to \(x^{\mathsf T}Q_ix\le 0\) for indices in a set \(I\) and \(x^{\mathsf T}Q_jx=0\) for indices in a set \(E\), where every coefficient matrix belongs to \(\mathbb S^n\). Every defining function is homogeneous of degree two, so for every \(t\in\mathbb R\), its value at \(tx\) equals \(t^2\) times its value at \(x\). Consequently, the feasible set is invariant under real scaling.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A homogeneous QCQP uses only degree-two quadratic forms. Its feasible set is closed under real scaling because all constraints scale by the square of the multiplier.
assumptions_latex: \(Q_i\in\mathbb S^n\) for every objective or constraint index
\(I\) and \(E\) are finite disjoint index sets
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\) feasible implies \(tx\) feasible for every \(t\in\mathbb R\).

notation.meaning: real symmetric matrices of order n

source_refs.locator: 3.9 The GOP for Quadratically Constrained Problems p. 96

knowledge_statements.title: Real Symmetric QCQP
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Real-field QCQP represented by symmetric coefficient matrices.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A real symmetric QCQP optimizes over \(x\in\mathbb R^n\) an objective \(q_0(x)=x^{\mathsf T}Q_0x+2c_0^{\mathsf T}x+d_0\), subject to finitely many relations \(q_i(x)\le 0\) or \(q_i(x)=0\), where \(q_i(x)=x^{\mathsf T}Q_ix+2c_i^{\mathsf T}x+d_i\), \(Q_i\in\mathbb S^n\), \(c_i\in\mathbb R^n\), and \(d_i\in\mathbb R\). Any real quadratic polynomial admits this representation because the skew-symmetric part of a matrix contributes zero to \(x^{\mathsf T}Q_ix\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A real symmetric QCQP has real variables and data, with every quadratic term represented by a real symmetric matrix.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(q_i(x)=x^{\mathsf T}Q_ix+2c_i^{\mathsf T}x+d_i\in\mathbb R\).

notation.meaning: real symmetric matrices of order n
real quadratic polynomial indexed by i

knowledge_statements.title: Complex Hermitian QCQP
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Complex-field QCQP whose quadratic functions are real-valued Hermitian forms.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A complex Hermitian QCQP optimizes over \(z\in\mathbb C^n\) a real-valued objective \(q_0(z)=z^*H_0z+2\operatorname{Re}(c_0^*z)+d_0\), subject to finitely many relations \(q_i(z)\le 0\) or \(q_i(z)=0\), where \(q_i(z)=z^*H_iz+2\operatorname{Re}(c_i^*z)+d_i\), \(H_i=H_i^*\in\mathbb C^{n\times n}\), \(c_i\in\mathbb C^n\), and \(d_i\in\mathbb R\). Hermitian symmetry ensures that every value \(z^*H_iz\) is real.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A complex Hermitian QCQP uses complex variables, Hermitian quadratic matrices, and real parts of affine terms so that all objectives and constraints are real-valued.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(q_i(z)=z^*H_iz+2\operatorname{Re}(c_i^*z)+d_i\in\mathbb R\).

notation.meaning: conjugate transpose of the matrix H_i

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The complex Hermitian formulation is mathematically plausible and fits the definition container, but no source or inspectable locator is supplied for the complex-field form, including its affine-term convention. An authoritative complex-QCQP reference is required.

knowledge_statements.title: Quadratic Inequality Systems
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Feasible regions defined exclusively by finitely many quadratic inequalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given quadratic functions \(q_i(x)=x^{\mathsf T}Q_ix+2c_i^{\mathsf T}x+d_i\) on \(\mathbb R^n\), a quadratic inequality system is
\[q_i(x)\le 0,\qquad i=1,\ldots,m.\]
Its feasible set is \(F=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:q_i(x)\le 0\text{ for all }i\}\). The matrices \(Q_i\in\mathbb S^n\) need not be positive semidefinite. Thus the definition includes both convex systems, when every \(Q_i\) is positive semidefinite, and potentially nonconvex systems otherwise.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A quadratic inequality system requires each of finitely many real quadratic functions to be nonpositive; indefinite constraint matrices may produce a nonconvex feasible set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F=\bigcap_{i=1}^m\{x\in\mathbb R^n:q_i(x)\le 0\}\).

notation.meaning: feasible set of the inequality system

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given quadratic functions \(q_i(x)=x^{\mathsf T}Q_ix+2c_i^{\mathsf T}x+d_i\) on \(\mathbb R^n\), a quadratic equality system is
\[q_i(x)=0,\qquad i=1,\ldots,m.\]
Its feasible set is the real algebraic set \(F=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:q_i(x)=0\text{ for all }i\}\). No definiteness condition is required of \(Q_i\in\mathbb S^n\), and the equations may be dependent or redundant unless an additional regularity assumption is imposed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A quadratic equality system is a finite collection of quadratic equations; its feasible points form a real algebraic set.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(q_k(x)=x^{\mathsf T}Q_kx+2c_k^{\mathsf T}x+d_k\) be real quadratic functions on \(\mathbb R^n\). A mixed quadratic equality-inequality system is
\[q_i(x)\le 0\quad(i\in I),\qquad q_j(x)=0\quad(j\in E),\]
where \(I\) and \(E\) are finite disjoint index sets. Its feasible set is \(F=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:q_i(x)\le0\text{ for all }i\in I,\ q_j(x)=0\text{ for all }j\in E\}\). Neither constraint family is required to be convex or independent.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A mixed quadratic system imposes quadratic inequalities and equations simultaneously, with feasibility requiring every relation in both indexed families.

knowledge_statements.title: Single Quadratic Constraint
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Constraint-count regime containing exactly one quadratic relation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A single-quadratic-constraint QCQP optimizes a quadratic function \(q_0:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) over a feasible set defined by exactly one quadratic relation. Its inequality form is
\[\operatorname*{minimize}_{x\in\mathbb R^n}q_0(x)\quad\text{subject to}\quad q_1(x)\le0,\]
and its equality form replaces the inequality by \(q_1(x)=0\). Each \(q_i(x)=x^{\mathsf T}Q_ix+2c_i^{\mathsf T}x+d_i\). Linear side constraints, if present, place the model outside this strict constraint-count convention unless explicitly excluded from the count.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: This regime has one quadratic objective and exactly one quadratic equality or inequality constraint, under the stated counting convention.
assumptions_latex: \(q_0\) and \(q_1\) are real quadratic functions on \(\mathbb R^n\)
Exactly one quadratic constraint is counted
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(m=1\) for the quadratic-constraint count.

source_refs.locator: 3.9 The GOP for Quadratically Constrained Problems p. 96

source_witnesses.locator: 3.9 The GOP for Quadratically Constrained Problems p. 96

knowledge_statements.title: Few Quadratic Constraints
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Parameterized regime where constraint count is fixed independently of variable dimension.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A family of QCQPs is in the few-quadratic-constraints regime when the total number \(m=|I|+|E|\) of quadratic inequalities and equalities is bounded by a constant \(k\) that does not depend on the variable dimension \(n\) or on the encoded instance size. Each instance may therefore have large \(n\), while satisfying \(m\le k\). The constant \(k\) is part of the family definition rather than part of each varying input; no convexity or definiteness is implied by this count restriction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A QCQP family has few quadratic constraints when their number is bounded by a fixed constant independent of dimension and input size.
assumptions_latex: \(k\in\mathbb N\) is fixed across the problem family
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(m=|I|+|E|\le k\) independently of \(n\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The fixed-parameter interpretation of 'few quadratic constraints' is coherent, but no source is supplied to establish that this exact asymptotic convention is intended by the leaf. A specific complexity or QCQP reference defining the family-wide constant bound is required.

knowledge_statements.title: General Quadratic Constraint Systems
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unrestricted constraint-count regime for finite QCQP systems.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A general quadratic constraint system consists of finitely many relations \(q_i(x)\le0\) for \(i\in I\) and \(q_j(x)=0\) for \(j\in E\), where every \(q_k:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) is quadratic. In this regime the total count \(m=|I|+|E|\) is part of the input and may grow with \(n\) or the encoded instance size. No uniform constant bound on \(m\), definiteness of the quadratic matrices, convexity, independence, or regularity of the constraints is included in the definition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A general quadratic constraint system permits any finite input-dependent number of quadratic equalities and inequalities, without implied convexity or regularity.
assumptions_latex: Every \(q_k\) is a real quadratic function on \(\mathbb R^n\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(m=|I|+|E|\) is unrestricted except for finiteness and may scale with the instance.

source_refs.locator: 3.9 The GOP for Quadratically Constrained Problems p. 96

source_witnesses.locator: 3.9 The GOP for Quadratically Constrained Problems p. 96

children.title: Feasible-Set Nonemptiness
children.top_down_role: Regimes in which the quadratic constraint system has at least one feasible point.

knowledge_statements.title: Feasible-Set Nonemptiness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Existential feasibility condition for a mixed QCQP constraint system.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For quadratic functions indexed by finite sets \(I\) and \(E\), define
\[F:=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:q_i(x)\le0\ \text{for every }i\in I,\ q_j(x)=0\ \text{for every }j\in E\}.\]
The system has a nonempty feasible set precisely when
\[\exists x\in\mathbb R^n\quad q_i(x)\le0\ \text{for all }i\in I\quad\text{and}\quad q_j(x)=0\ \text{for all }j\in E.\]
This condition asserts existence only; it does not require strict inequalities, interior points, boundedness, or attainment of an objective optimum.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A QCQP feasible set is nonempty exactly when at least one point satisfies every quadratic inequality and equality simultaneously.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\ne\varnothing\).

children.title: Strict Feasibility

knowledge_statements.title: Strict Feasibility
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Slater-type pointwise condition for quadratic inequalities with exact equalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For the mixed quadratic system \(q_i(x)\le0\) for \(i\in I\) and \(q_j(x)=0\) for \(j\in E\), a point \(\bar x\in\mathbb R^n\) is strictly feasible when
\[q_i(\bar x)<0\quad\text{for every }i\in I,\qquad q_j(\bar x)=0\quad\text{for every }j\in E.\]
The system is strictly feasible when such a point exists. Strictness applies only to inequality constraints; equality constraints remain exact. When \(I\) is empty, strict feasibility reduces to ordinary feasibility of the equality system.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strict feasibility means one point satisfies every quadratic inequality strictly and every quadratic equality exactly.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\exists\bar x\in\mathbb R^n\) such that \(q_i(\bar x)<0\) for all \(i\in I\) and \(q_j(\bar x)=0\) for all \(j\in E\).

children.title: Interior-Feasibility Gap
children.top_down_role: Nonempty feasible systems lacking strictly feasible points.

knowledge_statements.title: Interior-Feasibility Gap
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distinguishes feasible points from points satisfying every quadratic inequality strictly.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(q_i:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\), \(i=1,\ldots,m\), be quadratic functions. Define \(F=\{x:q_i(x)\leq 0\ \text{for all }i\}\) and \(F_{<}=\{x:q_i(x)<0\ \text{for all }i\}\). The interior-feasibility gap is \(G=F\setminus F_{<}\). Equivalently, \(x\in G\) exactly when \(x\in F\) and at least one constraint is active: \(q_i(x)=0\) for some \(i\). Thus \(G\) records feasible points not witnessed by strict feasibility; it need not equal the topological boundary of \(F\) when constraints are redundant or identically active.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The gap consists of feasible points at which at least one quadratic inequality is active, rather than all inequalities being strict.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(G=F\setminus F_{<}=\{x\in F:\exists i,\ q_i(x)=0\}\).

source_refs.locator: 1.3 Relative Interior and Closure p. 7

source_witnesses.locator: 1.3 Relative Interior and Closure p. 7

knowledge_statements.title: Boundary-Only Feasibility
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The nonempty regime in which no point satisfies all displayed inequalities strictly.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For quadratic inequalities \(q_i(x)\leq 0\), let \(F=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:q_i(x)\leq0\ \text{for every }i\}\). The system has boundary-only feasibility precisely when \(F\neq\varnothing\) and every \(x\in F\) activates at least one displayed constraint. Equivalently, \(F\neq\varnothing\) while \(\{x:q_i(x)<0\ \text{for every }i\}=\varnothing\). This condition concerns the displayed representation: adding a redundant equality encoded by two inequalities can create boundary-only feasibility without changing the underlying set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A system is boundary-only feasible when it has feasible points but every feasible point activates at least one displayed inequality.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\neq\varnothing\) and \(\forall x\in F\,\exists i:\ q_i(x)=0\).

notation.meaning: feasible set of the displayed quadratic inequalities

knowledge_statements.title: Infeasible Quadratic Systems
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Feasibility classification for a finite system of quadratic inequalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(q_i:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\), \(i=1,\ldots,m\), be quadratic functions. The quadratic system \(q_i(x)\leq0\) is infeasible if its common sublevel set is empty. In quantified form, infeasibility means that for every \(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\), at least one constraint is violated. This definition does not by itself provide a tractable certificate, and it applies whether the matrices defining the quadratics are positive semidefinite, indefinite, or negative semidefinite.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A quadratic system is infeasible when no point satisfies all its inequalities simultaneously.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:q_i(x)\leq0\ \forall i\}=\varnothing\), equivalently \(\forall x\,\exists i:\ q_i(x)>0\).

knowledge_statements.title: Compact Feasible Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional attainment for a continuous quadratic objective over a compact feasible set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:q_i(x)\leq0,\ i=1,\ldots,m\}\) be nonempty and compact, and let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) be quadratic. Since \(f\) is continuous, its restriction to \(F\) attains both extrema. Consequently, there exist \(x_{\min},x_{\max}\in F\) such that \(f(x_{\min})=\min_{x\in F}f(x)\) and \(f(x_{\max})=\max_{x\in F}f(x)\). In particular, the QCQP optimal value is finite and its minimizer set is a nonempty compact subset of \(F\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A continuous quadratic objective attains a finite minimum on every nonempty compact QCQP feasible set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in F}f(x)\) is nonempty and compact, and \(\min_{x\in F}f(x)\in\mathbb{R}\).

source_refs.locator: 2.13 Convex Optimization p. 76

source_witnesses.locator: 2.13 Convex Optimization p. 76

knowledge_statements.title: Coercive Objective Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Attainment on a closed feasible set under coercivity relative to that set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty and closed, and let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) be a quadratic function coercive on \(F\), meaning \(f(x_k)\to+\infty\) for every sequence \((x_k)\subset F\) with \(\lVert x_k\rVert\to\infty\). Then every nonempty lower level set \(\{x\in F:f(x)\leq\alpha\}\) is compact. Hence \(f\) is bounded below on \(F\), attains its minimum there, and \(\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in F}f(x)\) is nonempty and compact.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A quadratic objective coercive on a nonempty closed feasible set has compact lower levels and attains a finite minimum.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\min_{x\in F}f(x)\in\mathbb{R}\) exists and \(\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in F}f(x)\) is nonempty and compact.

children.title: Feasible Recession Directions
children.top_down_role: Directions that preserve feasibility asymptotically.

knowledge_statements.title: Feasible Recession Directions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Global recession directions of a possibly nonconvex QCQP feasible set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a nonempty set \(F\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\), a vector \(d\in\mathbb{R}^n\) is a feasible recession direction if every ray from every feasible point remains feasible: \(x+td\in F\) for all \(x\in F\) and all \(t\geq0\). The collection is the recession cone \(\operatorname{rec}(F)\). For \(F=\{x:q_i(x)\leq0,\ i=1,\ldots,m\}\), this means \(q_i(x+td)\leq0\) for every \(x\in F\), every \(t\geq0\), and every \(i\). A nonzero such direction proves that \(F\) is unbounded.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible recession direction keeps every ray starting in the feasible set feasible; any nonzero such direction proves unboundedness.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{rec}(F)=\{d:x+td\in F\ \forall x\in F,\ \forall t\geq0\}\).

children.title: Objective Descent at Infinity
children.top_down_role: Recession behavior permitting indefinitely improving objective values.

knowledge_statements.title: Objective Descent at Infinity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact descent test for a quadratic objective along a feasible ray.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f(x)=x^{\mathsf T}Hx+2g^{\mathsf T}x+\gamma\), with \(H=H^{\mathsf T}\), and suppose \(x+td\) is feasible for every \(t\geq0\). Along this ray, \(f(x+td)=f(x)+2t\,d^{\mathsf T}(Hx+g)+t^2d^{\mathsf T}Hd\). The objective descends to negative infinity along the ray exactly when either \(d^{\mathsf T}Hd<0\), or \(d^{\mathsf T}Hd=0\) and \(d^{\mathsf T}(Hx+g)<0\). Under either condition, \(f(x+td)\to-\infty\) as \(t\to\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Along a feasible ray, a negative quadratic coefficient—or a zero quadratic coefficient with negative linear coefficient—drives the objective to negative infinity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f(x+td)\to-\infty\) iff \(d^{\mathsf T}Hd<0\), or \(d^{\mathsf T}Hd=0\) and \(d^{\mathsf T}(Hx+g)<0\).

notation.meaning: objective Hessian matrix up to the factor two

knowledge_statements.title: Unbounded Optimal-Value Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A feasible-ray certificate that the minimization value equals negative infinity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(\inf\{f(y):y\in F\}\), where \(F\neq\varnothing\) and \(f\) is quadratic. A pair \((x,d)\) is an unbounded-value certificate when \(x\in F\), \(x+td\in F\) for every \(t\geq0\), and \(f(x+td)\to-\infty\). Such a pair certifies \(\inf_{y\in F}f(y)=-\infty\). For \(f(y)=y^{\mathsf T}Hy+2g^{\mathsf T}y+\gamma\), the final condition is verifiable by checking \(d^{\mathsf T}Hd<0\), or \(d^{\mathsf T}Hd=0\) together with \(d^{\mathsf T}(Hx+g)<0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible ray along which the quadratic objective tends to negative infinity certifies that the QCQP optimal value is unbounded below.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x+td\in F\ \forall t\geq0\) and \(f(x+td)\to-\infty\) imply \(\inf_{y\in F}f(y)=-\infty\).

notation.meaning: base point and direction of the certifying feasible ray

source_refs.locator: 3.9 The GOP for Quadratically Constrained Problems p. 96

source_witnesses.locator: 3.9 The GOP for Quadratically Constrained Problems p. 96

knowledge_statements.title: Ellipsoidal Regions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Completed-square representation of a bounded convex quadratic sublevel set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Q\in\mathbb{S}_{++}^n\) and \(q(x)=x^{\mathsf T}Qx+2b^{\mathsf T}x+c\). With \(x_c=-Q^{-1}b\) and \(\rho=b^{\mathsf T}Q^{-1}b-c\), the sublevel region satisfies \(\{x:q(x)\leq0\}=\{x:(x-x_c)^{\mathsf T}Q(x-x_c)\leq\rho\}\). It is a full-dimensional ellipsoid when \(\rho>0\), the singleton \(\{x_c\}\) when \(\rho=0\), and empty when \(\rho<0\). Thus positive definiteness yields a bounded convex quadratic region whenever the sublevel set is nonempty.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A positive-definite quadratic inequality becomes a centered ellipsoid after completing the square, with its radius parameter determining ellipsoid, singleton, or emptiness.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\{q\leq0\}=\{x:(x-x_c)^{\mathsf T}Q(x-x_c)\leq\rho\}\).

notation.meaning: squared-radius parameter in the Q metric

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The completed-square representation and the three cases determined by the sign of the radius parameter are mathematically consistent, but the record supplies no citation or inspectable locator.

children.title: Parabolic Quadratic Regions
children.top_down_role: Quadratic regions with parabolic cross-sectional geometry.

knowledge_statements.title: Parabolic Quadratic Regions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical decomposition when a singular convex quadratic has a linear null-space component.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Q\succeq0\) be singular and \(q(x)=x^{\mathsf T}Qx+2b^{\mathsf T}x+c\). Decompose \(b=b_R+b_N\) with \(b_R\in\operatorname{range}(Q)\) and nonzero \(b_N\in\ker(Q)\), and write \(x=u+v\) with \(u\in\operatorname{range}(Q)\), \(v\in\ker(Q)\). Then \(q(x)\leq0\) is equivalent to \((u+Q^{\dagger}b_R)^{\mathsf T}Q(u+Q^{\dagger}b_R)+2b_N^{\mathsf T}v\leq b_R^{\mathsf T}Q^{\dagger}b_R-c\). This is a convex parabolic quadratic region, possibly with free null directions orthogonal to \(b_N\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A singular positive-semidefinite quadratic with a nonzero linear null-space component has a parabolic completed-square representation.
assumptions_latex: \(b_N\), the projection of \(b\) onto \(\ker(Q)\), is nonzero.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(q(x)\leq0\) has the displayed parabolic range-null-space representation.

notation.meaning: range and null-space components of b
range and null-space components of x

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The range–kernel decomposition and completed-square formula are consistent, but the parabolic classification and free-null-direction statement have no cited source or locator.

children.title: Cylindrical Quadratic Regions
children.top_down_role: Quadratic regions possessing unconstrained axial directions.

knowledge_statements.title: Cylindrical Quadratic Regions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Ellipsoidal-cylinder representation for a singular convex quadratic without null-space drift.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Q\succeq0\) be nonzero and singular, let \(b\in\operatorname{range}(Q)\), and define \(q(x)=x^{\mathsf T}Qx+2b^{\mathsf T}x+c\). Set \(x_c=-Q^{\dagger}b\) and \(\rho=b^{\mathsf T}Q^{\dagger}b-c\). Then \(q(x)\leq0\) is equivalent to \((x-x_c)^{\mathsf T}Q(x-x_c)\leq\rho\). When \(\rho>0\), this is an ellipsoidal cylinder: its bounded cross-section lies in \(\operatorname{range}(Q)\), while every direction in \(\ker(Q)\) is free, so its recession cone equals \(\ker(Q)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible singular positive-semidefinite quadratic with no linear null-space component defines an ellipsoidal cylinder along the kernel.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\{q\leq0\}=\{x:(x-x_c)^{\mathsf T}Q(x-x_c)\leq\rho\}\) and \(\operatorname{rec}(\{q\leq0\})=\ker(Q)\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The ellipsoidal-cylinder representation and recession subspace claim are mathematically consistent under the stated positive-radius assumptions, but no supporting citation or locator is supplied.

children.title: Degenerate Quadratic Regions
children.top_down_role: Lower-dimensional or singular regions produced by degenerate quadratic data.

knowledge_statements.title: Degenerate Quadratic Regions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Lower-dimensional and empty endpoint cases of singular convex quadratic sublevel regions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Q\succeq0\) be singular, \(b\in\operatorname{range}(Q)\), \(q(x)=x^{\mathsf T}Qx+2b^{\mathsf T}x+c\), \(x_c=-Q^{\dagger}b\), and \(\rho=b^{\mathsf T}Q^{\dagger}b-c\). If \(\rho=0\), then \(\{x:q(x)\leq0\}=x_c+\ker(Q)\), an affine subspace. If \(\rho<0\), the region is empty. In the exceptional constant case \(Q=0\) and \(b=0\), the region is \(\mathbb{R}^n\) when \(c\leq0\) and empty when \(c>0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At zero radius a singular convex quadratic region collapses to an affine subspace; negative radius makes it empty, while constant inequalities give all space or emptiness.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\rho=0\Rightarrow\{q\leq0\}=x_c+\ker(Q)\), while \(\rho<0\Rightarrow\{q\leq0\}=\varnothing\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The zero-radius, negative-radius, and constant-quadratic cases are stated consistently, but the geometric classification lacks any source and inspectable locator.

assumptions_latex: The quadratic function is \(q(x)=x^{\mathsf T}Qx+2c^{\mathsf T}x+d\) on \(\mathbb R^n\), where \(Q\succeq 0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(R_q\) is the complement of the open convex set \(\{x:q(x)<0\}\), although \(R_q\) itself need not be convex.

notation.meaning: Convex quadratic function defining the region.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses the standard complement-of-convex-sublevel meaning of reverse convexity.

source_refs.locator: 7. Primal Methods in Reverse Convex Programming p. 172
1.2 Convex Sets p. 5

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a convex quadratic function \(q:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\), its reverse-convex quadratic region at level zero is
\[
R_q:=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:q(x)\ge 0\}=\mathbb R^n\setminus\{x\in\mathbb R^n:q(x)<0\}.
\]
The strict sublevel set \(\{x:q(x)<0\}\) is open and convex. Thus \(R_q\) is its complement and need not be convex. If the strict sublevel set is empty, then \(R_q=\mathbb R^n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A reverse-convex quadratic region is a convex quadratic's superlevel set, equivalently the complement of its open convex sublevel set.
knowledge_statements.title: Reverse-Convex Quadratic Regions

source_witnesses.locator: 7. Primal Methods in Reverse Convex Programming p. 172
1.2 Convex Sets p. 5

children.title: Hyperbolic Quadratic Regions
children.top_down_role: One-sheet, two-sheet, and related hyperbolic feasible-region geometries.

assumptions_latex: The quadratic Hessian is nonsingular and indefinite, with inertia \((p,r)\), where \(p\ge 1\) and \(r\ge 1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: After an invertible affine change of variables, each level inequality has the canonical form \(\|u\|_2^2-\|v\|_2^2\le \rho\) or its reverse.

notation.meaning: Coordinates associated with positive and negative quadratic directions.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Covers nondegenerate indefinite quadratics under affine congruence.

source_refs.locator: 3.9 The GOP for Quadratically Constrained Problems p. 96

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(q(x)=x^{\mathsf T}Qx+2c^{\mathsf T}x+d\), with symmetric, nonsingular, indefinite \(Q\). Completing the square and applying Sylvester congruence yields an invertible affine substitution \(x=x_0+T(u,v)\) and a scalar \(\rho\) such that
\[
q(x)\le 0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \|u\|_2^2-\|v\|_2^2\le \rho.
\]
Thus a hyperbolic quadratic region is an affine image of this canonical sublevel region; reversing the original inequality produces the corresponding canonical superlevel region.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every nondegenerate indefinite quadratic inequality is affinely equivalent to a difference-of-squared-norms inequality, which defines a hyperbolic quadratic region.
knowledge_statements.title: Hyperbolic Quadratic Regions

source_witnesses.locator: 3.9 The GOP for Quadratically Constrained Problems p. 96

children.title: Saddle Quadratic Regions
children.top_down_role: Indefinite regions governed by opposing curvature directions.

assumptions_latex: The symmetric quadratic matrix \(Q\) has at least one positive and at least one negative eigenvalue.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The function \(q\) has both upward- and downward-curving directions, so its level regions are indefinite quadratic regions.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses Hessian inertia to define saddle geometry, including singular indefinite cases.

source_refs.locator: 3.9 The GOP for Quadratically Constrained Problems p. 96

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A saddle quadratic region at level \(\alpha\in\mathbb R\) is a set
\[
S_\alpha:=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:q(x)\le \alpha\},
\]
where \(q(x)=x^{\mathsf T}Qx+2c^{\mathsf T}x+d\) and the symmetric matrix \(Q\) is indefinite. Equivalently, there exist nonzero directions \(h_+\) and \(h_-\) satisfying \(h_+^{\mathsf T}Qh_+>0\) and \(h_-^{\mathsf T}Qh_-<0\). Hence the quadratic has opposite curvature signs along suitable lines.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A saddle quadratic region is a level region of a quadratic whose Hessian has both positive and negative curvature directions.
knowledge_statements.title: Saddle Quadratic Regions

source_witnesses.locator: 3.9 The GOP for Quadratically Constrained Problems p. 96

children.title: Hyperbolic Connectivity Regimes
children.top_down_role: Connectivity changes across hyperbolic quadratic-region variants.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(H_\rho\) is connected for \(\rho\ge0\); for \(\rho<0\), it has two components exactly when \(r=1\), and is connected when \(r\ge2\).

notation.meaning: Numbers of positive and negative squared coordinates.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classifies connectivity of the canonical sublevel form; superlevels follow by exchanging inertia indices.

source_refs.locator: 3.9 The GOP for Quadratically Constrained Problems p. 96

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For
\[
H_\rho:=\{(u,v)\in\mathbb R^p\times\mathbb R^r:\|u\|_2^2-\|v\|_2^2\le\rho\},
\]
if \(\rho\ge0\), then \(H_\rho\) is path connected. If \(\rho<0\), then \(H_\rho\) has exactly two path components when \(r=1\), distinguished by the sign of the scalar \(v\), whereas it is path connected when \(r\ge2\). For the reversed inequality, the same classification holds after exchanging \(p\) and \(r\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Hyperbolic connectivity depends on the level sign and the dimension of the squared-norm block forced away from zero.
knowledge_statements.title: Hyperbolic Connectivity Regimes

source_witnesses.locator: 3.9 The GOP for Quadratically Constrained Problems p. 96

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The quadratic region \(D_a\) is the disjoint union of two nonempty path-connected components.

notation.meaning: Positive-curvature coordinates and the separating scalar coordinate.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gives the canonical two-sheeted hyperbolic mechanism for disconnection.

source_refs.locator: 3.9 The GOP for Quadratically Constrained Problems p. 96

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(a>0\) and \(p\ge1\), define
\[
D_a:=\{(u,t)\in\mathbb R^p\times\mathbb R:\|u\|_2^2-t^2\le-a^2\}.
\]
This region has exactly two path components,
\[
D_a^+:=D_a\cap\{t\ge a\},\qquad D_a^-:=D_a\cap\{t\le-a\},
\]
and \(D_a=D_a^+\mathbin{\dot\cup}D_a^-\). Both components are nonempty and path connected. Every invertible affine image of \(D_a\) has the same two-component structure.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A two-sheeted hyperbolic inequality defines two nonempty path-connected components, and invertible affine changes preserve this disconnection.
knowledge_statements.title: Disconnected Quadratic Regions

source_witnesses.locator: 3.9 The GOP for Quadratically Constrained Problems p. 96

assumptions_latex: The quadratic function is \(q(x)=x^{\mathsf T}Qx+2c^{\mathsf T}x+d\) with symmetric \(Q\).
For the manifold conclusion, \(2Qx+2c\ne0\) at every \(x\) satisfying \(q(x)=0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Under the regularity condition, \(M=\{x:q(x)=0\}\) is a smooth embedded submanifold of dimension \(n-1\).

notation.meaning: Normal vector to the level set.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines quadratic equality sets and states the regular-level manifold condition.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 2 The Method of Multipliers for Equality Constrained Problems
source_refs.source_title: Constrained Optimization and Lagrange Multiplier Methods

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A quadratic equality set is
\[
M:=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:q(x)=0\},
\]
where \(q(x)=x^{\mathsf T}Qx+2c^{\mathsf T}x+d\) and \(Q\) is symmetric. It is a quadratic equality manifold when zero is a regular value of \(q\), namely when \(\nabla q(x)=2Qx+2c\ne0\) for every \(x\in M\). Under this condition, \(M\) is a smooth embedded hypersurface, its dimension is \(n-1\), and its tangent space is \(T_xM=\{h:\nabla q(x)^{\mathsf T}h=0\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A regular quadratic equality level set is a smooth hypersurface whose tangent space is orthogonal to the quadratic gradient.
knowledge_statements.title: Quadratic Equality Manifolds

source_witnesses.locator: Chapter 2 The Method of Multipliers for Equality Constrained Problems
source_witnesses.source_title: Constrained Optimization and Lagrange Multiplier Methods

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The regular-level-set statement is mathematically standard and correctly formulated, but the citation gives only an entire chapter and no section, theorem, definition, or page locator. A specific source location supporting the regular-value manifold and tangent-space claims is required.

children.title: Diagonal QCQP Data
children.top_down_role: QCQP instances whose quadratic matrices are diagonal in the working coordinates.

assumptions_latex: A QCQP has quadratic functions \(q_i(x)=x^{\mathsf T}Q_i x+2c_i^{\mathsf T}x+d_i\) for \(i=0,\ldots,m\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The data are diagonal exactly when every \(Q_i\) is diagonal in the stated coordinate system.

notation.meaning: Diagonal entries of the quadratic matrices.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Diagonal means diagonal in the given coordinates, not merely diagonalizable after transformation.

source_refs.locator: 3.9 The GOP for Quadratically Constrained Problems p. 96

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A QCQP has diagonal quadratic data in a fixed coordinate system when each symmetric matrix \(Q_i\), including the objective matrix \(Q_0\), is diagonal. Equivalently, every quadratic function has the form
\[
q_i(x)=\sum_{j=1}^n a_{ij}x_j^2+2\sum_{j=1}^n c_{ij}x_j+d_i,
\]
with no product \(x_jx_k\) for \(j\ne k\). The linear coefficients \(c_{ij}\) and constants \(d_i\) are unrestricted.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Diagonal QCQP data contain only coordinate squares, linear terms, and constants; no quadratic term multiplies two distinct coordinates.
knowledge_statements.title: Diagonal QCQP Data

source_witnesses.locator: 3.9 The GOP for Quadratically Constrained Problems p. 96

children.title: Coordinate-Separable QCQP
children.top_down_role: QCQP instances decomposable across individual variables or coordinate blocks.

assumptions_latex: The QCQP functions are defined on a Cartesian domain \(X=X_1\times\cdots\times X_n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The QCQP is coordinate-separable exactly when every objective and constraint function is an additive sum of univariate coordinate functions plus a constant.

notation.meaning: Univariate contribution of coordinate \(j\) to function \(i\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Additive function separability does not imply that multiple inequality constraints decouple into independent scalar problems.

source_refs.locator: 3.9 The GOP for Quadratically Constrained Problems p. 96

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A QCQP is coordinate-separable on \(X=X_1\times\cdots\times X_n\) when, for every \(i=0,\ldots,m\), there are univariate quadratic functions \(\phi_{ij}:X_j\to\mathbb R\) and constants \(d_i\) such that
\[
q_i(x)=d_i+\sum_{j=1}^n\phi_{ij}(x_j).
\]
For quadratic functions on a full-dimensional Cartesian domain, this holds if and only if every \(Q_i\) is diagonal in the same fixed coordinates. The sums within constraints may still couple coordinate choices through their common inequality bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A coordinate-separable QCQP expresses every objective and constraint as a sum of univariate quadratic coordinate contributions.
knowledge_statements.title: Coordinate-Separable QCQP

source_witnesses.locator: 3.9 The GOP for Quadratically Constrained Problems p. 96

children.title: Residual Coupling Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Structures that remain diagonal-like but retain coupling that prevents full separability.

assumptions_latex: The quadratic functions are represented by symmetric matrices \(Q_i\) in fixed coordinates.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Exact coordinate separability holds if and only if \((Q_i)_{jk}=0\) for every \(i\) and every \(j\ne k\).

notation.meaning: Mixed second derivative between coordinates \(j\) and \(k\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Identifies the exact algebraic boundary of additive coordinate separability.

source_refs.locator: 3.9 The GOP for Quadratically Constrained Problems p. 96

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Write \(Q_i=\operatorname{Diag}(Q_i)+R_i\), where \(R_i\) has zero diagonal. The quadratic contribution from the residual is
\[
x^{\mathsf T}R_i x=2\sum_{1\le j<k\le n}(Q_i)_{jk}x_jx_k.
\]
On any full-dimensional Cartesian domain, additive coordinate separability of every \(q_i\) holds exactly when \(R_i=0\) for all \(i\). Thus a single nonzero off-diagonal coefficient is the boundary: it introduces a mixed derivative and prevents representation as a sum of univariate coordinate functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Off-diagonal quadratic coefficients are precisely the residual interactions that destroy additive coordinate separability on a full-dimensional Cartesian domain.
knowledge_statements.title: Residual Coupling Boundaries

source_witnesses.locator: 3.9 The GOP for Quadratically Constrained Problems p. 96

assumptions_latex: The matrices \(Q_0,\ldots,Q_m\) are real and symmetric.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A common orthogonal diagonalizer exists if and only if the matrices commute pairwise.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: States simultaneous orthogonal diagonalization for a finite family of real symmetric matrices.

source_refs.locator: 3.9 The GOP for Quadratically Constrained Problems p. 96

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A QCQP is simultaneously orthogonally diagonalizable when there exists an orthogonal matrix \(U\) such that \(D_i=U^{\mathsf T}Q_iU\) is diagonal for every \(i=0,\ldots,m\). Under the substitution \(x=Uy\),
\[
q_i(Uy)=y^{\mathsf T}D_i y+2(U^{\mathsf T}c_i)^{\mathsf T}y+d_i,
\]
so the transformed QCQP has diagonal quadratic data. For real symmetric matrices, such a common \(U\) exists if and only if \(Q_iQ_k=Q_kQ_i\) for every pair \(i,k\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A symmetric QCQP becomes diagonally quadratic under one orthogonal change of variables exactly when all its quadratic matrices commute pairwise.
knowledge_statements.title: Simultaneously Diagonalizable QCQP

source_witnesses.locator: 3.9 The GOP for Quadratically Constrained Problems p. 96

children.title: Bilinear QCQP Interactions
children.top_down_role: Quadratic models dominated by cross-products between variable groups.

assumptions_latex: Variables are partitioned as \(x=(u,v)\in\mathbb R^p\times\mathbb R^r\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The cross-block quadratic term is \(u^{\mathsf T}B_i v\), represented by a symmetric matrix with off-diagonal blocks \(B_i/2\) and \(B_i^{\mathsf T}/2\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses the symmetric-matrix convention for embedding rectangular bilinear terms in a QCQP.

source_refs.locator: 3.9 The GOP for Quadratically Constrained Problems p. 96

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A bilinear interaction between variable blocks \(u\in\mathbb R^p\) and \(v\in\mathbb R^r\) is a term \(u^{\mathsf T}B_i v\). With \(x=(u,v)\), it has the symmetric quadratic representation
\[
u^{\mathsf T}B_i v=x^{\mathsf T}\begin{pmatrix}0&B_i/2\\B_i^{\mathsf T}/2&0\end{pmatrix}x.
\]
Consequently, a purely bilinear QCQP function has no within-block quadratic terms; it may additionally contain arbitrary linear terms in \(u\) and \(v\) and a constant.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bilinear QCQP interaction multiplies variables from two blocks and occupies only the cross-block portions of the symmetric quadratic matrix.
knowledge_statements.title: Bilinear QCQP Interactions

source_witnesses.locator: 3.9 The GOP for Quadratically Constrained Problems p. 96

children.title: Bipartite Variable Partitions
children.top_down_role: QCQP interaction graphs admitting a bipartite variable partition.

assumptions_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be the aggregate interaction graph, with \(\{j,k\}\in E\) when some \((Q_i)_{jk}\ne0\) for \(j\ne k\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A bipartite variable partition exists exactly when \(G\) is bipartite, equivalently when \(G\) has no odd cycle.

notation.meaning: Aggregate graph of cross-variable quadratic interactions.
Two parts of the variable-index partition.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: The partition is common to all objective and constraint matrices.

source_refs.locator: 3.9 The GOP for Quadratically Constrained Problems p. 96

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A bipartite variable partition for a QCQP is a decomposition \(V=L\mathbin{\dot\cup}R\) of coordinate indices such that every off-diagonal quadratic interaction joins one index in \(L\) to one in \(R\). Equivalently, after one common permutation of coordinates, each quadratic matrix has the form
\[
Q_i=\begin{pmatrix}D_{i,L}&B_i/2\\B_i^{\mathsf T}/2&D_{i,R}\end{pmatrix},
\]
where \(D_{i,L}\) and \(D_{i,R}\) are diagonal. Such a partition exists if and only if the aggregate interaction graph is bipartite, equivalently contains no odd cycle.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A common bipartite partition places every mixed quadratic interaction across two coordinate classes; it exists exactly when the aggregate interaction graph has no odd cycle.
knowledge_statements.title: Bipartite Variable Partitions

source_witnesses.locator: 3.9 The GOP for Quadratically Constrained Problems p. 96

children.title: Nonbipartite Coupling Boundary
children.top_down_role: Bilinear interaction patterns that fail bipartite structural separation.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonbipartite Coupling Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Graph-theoretic boundary for separating all QCQP bilinear interactions across two variable blocks.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For symmetric quadratic data matrices \(Q_0,\ldots,Q_m\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\), define the coupling graph \(G=(V,E)\) by \(V=\{1,\ldots,n\}\) and \(\{j,k\}\in E\) exactly when \(j\ne k\) and \((Q_i)_{jk}\ne0\) for some \(i\). A partition \(V=V_1\mathbin{\dot\cup}V_2\) placing every coupled pair in different blocks exists if and only if \(G\) is bipartite. Equivalently, such a bilinear-bipartite representation fails exactly when \(G\) contains an odd cycle.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The coupling family ceases to be bipartite exactly when its aggregate interaction graph contains an odd cycle.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(G\text{ is nonbipartite}\iff G\text{ contains an odd cycle}.\)

notation.meaning: Aggregate graph of off-diagonal quadratic interactions.
Candidate bipartition of the variable indices.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard odd-cycle characterization of bipartite graphs applied to the QCQP coupling graph

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary formulation and odd-cycle characterization are mathematically precise and fit the leaf, but no inspectable source with a specific locator is supplied.

knowledge_statements.title: Aggregate Sparsity Graphs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Union sparsity pattern of every quadratic form in a QCQP.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given symmetric QCQP matrices \(Q_0,\ldots,Q_m\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\), their aggregate sparsity graph is the undirected graph \(G=(V,E)\) with \(V=\{1,\ldots,n\}\) and \[E=\bigl\{\{j,k\}:1\le j<k\le n,\ (Q_i)_{jk}\ne0\text{ for at least one }i\in\{0,\ldots,m\}\bigr\}.\] Thus every off-diagonal nonzero appearing in any objective or constraint matrix is represented, while diagonal entries correspond to vertices rather than edges.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The aggregate sparsity graph is the union of the off-diagonal sparsity patterns of all objective and constraint matrices.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(E=\bigcup_{i=0}^{m}\operatorname{supp}_{\mathrm{off}}(Q_i).\)

notation.meaning: Unordered index pairs of nonzero off-diagonal entries of Q.

source_refs.locator: 4.1.1 Structure and Sparsity p. 56

source_witnesses.locator: 4.1.1 Structure and Sparsity p. 56

children.title: Chordal Sparsity Patterns
children.top_down_role: Chordal graph structure arising from aggregate QCQP sparsity.

knowledge_statements.title: Chordal Sparsity Patterns
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Chordality of the aggregate graph supporting sparse matrix decomposition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A symmetric sparsity pattern on \(V=\{1,\ldots,n\}\) is chordal when its undirected graph \(G=(V,E)\) has no induced cycle of length at least four. Equivalently, there is an ordering \(v_1,\ldots,v_n\) such that, for every \(k\), the higher-numbered neighbors of \(v_k\) form a clique. Such an ordering is called a perfect elimination ordering and may be used to organize clique-based sparse matrix representations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A sparsity pattern is chordal when every cycle of length at least four has a chord, equivalently when it admits perfect elimination.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is a finite undirected graph representing a symmetric matrix pattern.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(G\text{ is chordal}\iff G\text{ admits a perfect elimination ordering}.\)

notation.meaning: Undirected graph of the symmetric sparsity pattern.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard equivalent definitions of finite chordal graphs

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The equivalent chordality definitions are standard, internally consistent, and appropriate for this leaf, but no inspectable citation with a specific locator is supplied.

children.title: Maximal Clique Decompositions
children.top_down_role: Clique-based decomposition of sparse lifted or conic representations.

knowledge_statements.title: Maximal Clique Decompositions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Decomposition of a chordally sparse positive-semidefinite matrix over maximal cliques.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be chordal with maximal cliques \(C_1,\ldots,C_p\), and let \(E_k\) select the coordinates indexed by \(C_k\). The cone of positive-semidefinite matrices having zeros outside the diagonal and edges of \(G\) satisfies \[\mathbb S_+^n(G)=\left\{\sum_{k=1}^{p}E_k^{\mathsf T}Z_kE_k: Z_k\in\mathbb S_+^{|C_k|}\right\}.\] Hence a chordally sparse positive-semidefinite matrix can be represented as a sum of positive-semidefinite matrices supported on maximal cliques.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every positive-semidefinite matrix with chordal sparsity is a sum of positive-semidefinite matrices embedded on the maximal cliques.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb S_+^n(G)=\sum_{k=1}^{p}E_k^{\mathsf T}\mathbb S_+^{|C_k|}E_k.\)

notation.meaning: Positive-semidefinite matrices whose off-diagonal support is contained in G.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard chordal sparse positive-semidefinite cone decomposition

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The chordal sparse positive-semidefinite cone representation is correctly distinguished from the partial-matrix completion formulation, but this nontrivial representation theorem requires a specifically located source.

children.title: Clique Separator Consistency
children.top_down_role: Consistency requirements across overlapping clique representations.

knowledge_statements.title: Clique Separator Consistency
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Overlap equations required to assemble clique-local matrices into one chordal partial matrix.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let maximal cliques \(C_1,\ldots,C_p\) of a chordal graph be arranged as a clique tree \(T\), and assign a symmetric matrix \(Z_k\) to each clique. For every tree edge \((k,\ell)\), put \(S_{k\ell}=C_k\cap C_\ell\). The clique matrices are separator-consistent precisely when \[(Z_k)_{S_{k\ell},S_{k\ell}}=(Z_\ell)_{S_{k\ell},S_{k\ell}}\quad\text{for every }(k,\ell)\in T.\] These equations are necessary and sufficient for the clique matrices to be restrictions of a common symmetric partial matrix on the chordal pattern.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Neighboring clique matrices must agree on every separator; these equalities exactly permit assembly into one partial matrix.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is chordal and \(T\) is a clique tree of its maximal cliques.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\exists Z\text{ with }Z[C_k,C_k]=Z_k\ \forall k\iff Z_k[S_{k\ell},S_{k\ell}]=Z_\ell[S_{k\ell},S_{k\ell}]\ \forall(k,\ell)\in T.\)

notation.meaning: Clique tree satisfying the running-intersection property.
Symmetric matrix local to clique C_k.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: running-intersection property reduces global overlap consistency to clique-tree separators

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The separator equations and common-partial-matrix conclusion are precise under the clique-tree assumption, but their necessity and sufficiency require a specifically located supporting theorem.

children.title: Low-Rank Quadratic Data
children.top_down_role: QCQP families with low-rank objective or constraint matrices.

knowledge_statements.title: Low-Rank Quadratic Data
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Factorized representation of rank-deficient symmetric QCQP matrices.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A symmetric quadratic matrix \(Q\in\mathbb S^n\) has rank \(r\) if and only if there exist a full-column-rank matrix \(U\in\mathbb R^{n\times r}\) and a nonsingular symmetric matrix \(S\in\mathbb S^r\) such that \(Q=USU^{\mathsf T}\). Consequently, \[x^{\mathsf T}Qx=(U^{\mathsf T}x)^{\mathsf T}S(U^{\mathsf T}x),\] so the quadratic term depends on \(x\) only through \(r\) linear projections. If \(Q\succeq0\), the factorization may be chosen with \(S=I_r\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A rank-r quadratic form factors through r linear projections; for positive-semidefinite data it is a squared norm of those projections.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Q=USU^{\mathsf T}\quad\text{and}\quad x^{\mathsf T}Qx=(U^{\mathsf T}x)^{\mathsf T}S(U^{\mathsf T}x).\)
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: spectral factorization of a finite-dimensional symmetric matrix

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The rank factorization, induced quadratic representation, and positive-semidefinite specialization are mathematically sound and fit the representation leaf, but no inspectable source is supplied.

children.title: Symmetry Structure
children.top_down_role: Invariant QCQP data supporting symmetry-based reduction or classification.

knowledge_statements.title: Symmetry Structure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite orthogonal group invariance of QCQP data, feasibility, and objective values.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a finite group \(\Gamma\) act on \(\mathbb R^n\) through orthogonal matrices \(P_g\). For quadratic functions \(f_i(x)=x^{\mathsf T}Q_ix+2q_i^{\mathsf T}x+c_i\), suppose \(P_g^{\mathsf T}Q_iP_g=Q_i\) and \(P_g^{\mathsf T}q_i=q_i\) for every \(g\in\Gamma\) and every \(i\). Then \(f_i(P_gx)=f_i(x)\). If the remaining domain is also \(\Gamma\)-invariant, every feasible point has a feasible orbit with a common objective value.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Invariant quadratic data and an invariant domain make feasibility and objective values constant along every group orbit.
assumptions_latex: The nonquadratic domain is invariant under \(x\mapsto P_gx\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f_i(P_gx)=f_i(x)\text{ for all }g,i,x,\) and feasible sets are unions of \(\Gamma\)-orbits.

notation.meaning: Orthogonal representation matrix for group element g.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: direct invariance criterion for quadratic functions under orthogonal group actions

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The stated invariance conditions correctly imply constancy of every quadratic function and feasibility along group orbits, but the property has no specifically located citation.

children.title: Sign-Structured Quadratics
children.top_down_role: Quadratic data with exploitable coefficient or interaction sign patterns.

knowledge_statements.title: Sign-Structured Quadratics
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quadratic matrices whose off-diagonal coefficients obey a prescribed sign pattern.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix an undirected interaction set \(E\) and a sign assignment \(\sigma:E\to\{-1,+1\}\). A symmetric matrix \(Q\in\mathbb S^n\) is sign-structured with respect to \((E,\sigma)\) when \(Q_{jk}=0\) for \(\{j,k\}\notin E\) and \[\sigma_{jk}Q_{jk}\ge0\quad\text{for every }\{j,k\}\in E.\] Its diagonal entries are unrestricted unless additional curvature conditions are imposed. The associated quadratic form therefore has a fixed permitted sign for every bilinear interaction coefficient.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A sign-structured quadratic has zero interactions outside a chosen graph and prescribed signs on all interactions within it.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Q\in\mathcal S(E,\sigma)\iff Q_{jk}=0\text{ off }E\text{ and }\sigma_{jk}Q_{jk}\ge0\text{ on }E.\)

notation.meaning: Class of matrices satisfying the sign pattern.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: explicit local definition of a prescribed signed sparsity class

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The signed sparsity class is explicitly and consistently defined, but the intended field meaning of “sign-structured quadratics” is not supported by an inspectable source.

children.title: Mixed Structural Regimes
children.top_down_role: QCQP families combining rank, symmetry, or sign restrictions.

knowledge_statements.title: Mixed Structural Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Simultaneous membership of quadratic data in multiple exact structural classes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal S_G\subseteq\mathbb S^n\) denote matrices supported on a graph \(G\), \(\mathcal R_r=\{Q\in\mathbb S^n:\operatorname{rank}(Q)\le r\}\), and let \(\mathcal I_\Gamma\) and \(\mathcal S(E,\sigma)\) denote prescribed symmetry-invariant and sign-structured classes. A QCQP is in a mixed structural regime when each quadratic matrix \(Q_i\) is assigned to an explicitly stated intersection of at least two such classes, for example \[Q_i\in\mathcal S_G\cap\mathcal R_r\cap\mathcal I_\Gamma.\] No one structural descriptor is inferred from another.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A mixed regime requires each quadratic matrix to satisfy two or more independently stated structures, such as sparsity, low rank, symmetry, or signs.
assumptions_latex: All structural classes are subsets of the common ambient space \(\mathbb S^n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Q_i\in\bigcap_{a\in A_i}\mathcal C_a\quad\text{with}\quad |A_i|\ge2.\)

notation.meaning: Symmetric matrices supported on graph G.
Symmetric matrices of rank at most r.
Matrices invariant under the specified group action.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: set-intersection formulation makes simultaneous structural assumptions explicit

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The intersection-based definition is coherent and fits the mixed-structure leaf, but the proposed terminology and threshold of at least two classes lack a specifically located source.

knowledge_statements.title: Box-Constrained QCQP
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Continuous QCQP whose variable domain is a coordinate box.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A box-constrained QCQP has the form \[\min_{x\in\mathbb R^n}\ f_0(x)\quad\text{subject to}\quad f_i(x)\le0\ (i=1,\ldots,m),\qquad \ell\le x\le u,\] where \(f_i(x)=x^{\mathsf T}Q_ix+2q_i^{\mathsf T}x+c_i\), \(Q_i\in\mathbb S^n\), and the bound inequalities hold componentwise. With finite vectors \(\ell,u\in\mathbb R^n\) satisfying \(\ell\le u\), the box is nonempty and compact; neither the objective nor the quadratic constraints are required to be convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A box-constrained QCQP adds finite componentwise lower and upper bounds to quadratic objective and constraint functions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal F=\{x\in[\ell,u]:f_i(x)\le0,\ i=1,\ldots,m\}.\)

source_refs.locator: 3.9 The GOP for Quadratically Constrained Problems p. 96
Chapter 11. The alphaBB for Box Constrained Twice-Differentiable NLPs: Theory p. 315

knowledge_statements.title: Polyhedrally Constrained QCQP
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Continuous QCQP intersected with an explicitly represented polyhedron.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A polyhedrally constrained QCQP has the form \[\min_{x\in\mathbb R^n}\ f_0(x)\quad\text{subject to}\quad f_i(x)\le0\ (i=1,\ldots,m),\qquad Ax\le b,\] where \(f_i(x)=x^{\mathsf T}Q_ix+2q_i^{\mathsf T}x+c_i\) and \(Q_i\in\mathbb S^n\). Equalities may be included as pairs of linear inequalities. The polyhedral restriction does not by itself imply boundedness, and the quadratic functions may be convex or nonconvex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A polyhedrally constrained QCQP combines quadratic objective and constraints with finitely many linear inequalities.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal F=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:f_i(x)\le0\ \forall i,\ Ax\le b\}.\)

notation.meaning: Linear inequality data defining the polyhedron.

source_refs.locator: 1.2 Structure of Global Optimization Models p. 3

knowledge_statements.title: Conically Constrained QCQP
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Continuous QCQP augmented by affine membership in a closed convex cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^p\) be a closed convex cone. A conically constrained QCQP has the form \[\min_{x\in\mathbb R^n}\ f_0(x)\quad\text{subject to}\quad f_i(x)\le0\ (i=1,\ldots,m),\qquad Ax+b\in K,\] where \(f_i(x)=x^{\mathsf T}Q_ix+2q_i^{\mathsf T}x+c_i\) and \(Q_i\in\mathbb S^n\). The adjective conic refers to the affine conic restriction; the quadratic functions need not be convex unless additional semidefiniteness assumptions are imposed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A conically constrained QCQP adds an affine membership constraint in a specified closed convex cone.
assumptions_latex: \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^p\) is a closed convex cone.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal F=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:f_i(x)\le0\ \forall i,\ Ax+b\in K\}.\)

notation.meaning: Closed convex cone defining the conic restriction.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard affine-conic extension of a QCQP model

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The affine conic-domain extension is precise and internally consistent, but no inspectable source establishes that this is the intended standard scope of “conically constrained QCQP.”

assumptions_latex: Decision variables lie in a finite-dimensional Euclidean space and at least one component is restricted to an integer-valued set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The model is an MIQCQP rather than a continuous QCQP; continuous convex-QCQP theory applies only after fixing or relaxing the discrete variables.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Marks the modeling boundary between continuous QCQP and mixed-integer quadratic optimization.

source_refs.locator: 3.9 The GOP for Quadratically Constrained Problems p. 96
5.4 Bilevel Linear-Quadratic and Bilevel Quadratic-Quadratic Problems p. 187

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A mixed-integer quadratically constrained quadratic program has the form \[\min\{q_0(x,z):q_i(x,z)\le 0,\ i=1,\ldots,m,\ x\in\mathbb R^n,\ z\in Z\subseteq\mathbb Z^p\},\] where every \(q_i\) is quadratic in the combined vector \((x,z)\). Even when all continuous quadratic functions have positive-semidefinite Hessians, the set \(\mathbb R^n\times Z\) is discrete in the integer coordinates and hence is not a convex continuous domain unless \(Z\) is a singleton. Fixing \(z\) produces a continuous QCQP; replacing \(Z\) by a convex relaxation produces a relaxation, not an equivalent continuous model in general.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Integer restrictions move a quadratic model outside continuous QCQP theory. Fixing integer variables gives continuous QCQPs, while convexifying their domain generally yields only a relaxation.
knowledge_statements.title: Mixed-Integer QCQP Boundary

children.top_down_role: Recognition, equivalent conic representation, duality, optimality, and computational representation choices for convex QCQP.

assumptions_latex: The objective is \(q_0(x)=\tfrac12 x^{\mathsf T}Q_0x+c_0^{\mathsf T}x+d_0\), with \(Q_0\) symmetric.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The signs of the eigenvalues of \(Q_0\) completely determine the global curvature regime of the quadratic objective.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classifies a quadratic objective by the inertia of its symmetric Hessian.

source_refs.locator: 2.13 Convex Optimization p. 76

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(q_0(x)=\tfrac12 x^{\mathsf T}Q_0x+c_0^{\mathsf T}x+d_0\) with \(Q_0=Q_0^{\mathsf T}\), the objective is convex on \(\mathbb R^n\) exactly when \(Q_0\succeq0\), and strictly convex exactly when \(Q_0\succ0\). It is affine exactly when \(Q_0=0\). It is concave exactly when \(Q_0\preceq0\), and strictly concave exactly when \(Q_0\prec0\). If \(Q_0\) has both a positive and a negative eigenvalue, then \(q_0\) is neither convex nor concave on \(\mathbb R^n\). Thus minimization has a convex objective precisely in the positive-semidefinite regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A quadratic minimization objective is convex exactly when its symmetric Hessian is positive semidefinite; zero, negative-semidefinite, and indefinite Hessians give affine, concave, and saddle regimes.
knowledge_statements.title: Objective Curvature Regimes

source_witnesses.locator: 2.13 Convex Optimization p. 76

assumptions_latex: Each inequality is written as \(q_i(x)\le0\), where \(q_i(x)=\tfrac12x^{\mathsf T}Q_ix+c_i^{\mathsf T}x+d_i\) and \(Q_i\) is symmetric.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Positive-semidefinite constraint Hessians yield convex sublevel constraints; other curvature regimes do not provide this general convexity guarantee.

notation.meaning: symmetric Hessian of constraint function i
feasible sublevel set of constraint i

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses the standard sublevel orientation for QCQP inequalities.

source_refs.locator: 2.5 Convex Inequalities p. 52
2.6.4 Nonlinearly Constrained Convex Sets p. 127

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an inequality \(q_i(x)\le0\), the function \(q_i\) is convex on \(\mathbb R^n\) if and only if \(Q_i\succeq0\); in that regime its sublevel set \(C_i=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:q_i(x)\le0\}\) is convex. If \(Q_i=0\), the constraint is affine and its feasible set is a halfspace, possibly empty or all of \(\mathbb R^n\). A negative-semidefinite or indefinite \(Q_i\) does not generally yield a convex sublevel set. Consequently, a QCQP in standard inequality form is recognized as convex when every objective and inequality Hessian is positive semidefinite and all equality constraints are affine.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A standard quadratic inequality is a convex constraint when its Hessian is positive semidefinite. Affine constraints are included; negative-semidefinite or indefinite Hessians give no general convexity guarantee.
knowledge_statements.title: Constraint Curvature Regimes

children.title: Affine Quadratic Expressions
children.top_down_role: Objective or constraint expressions whose quadratic component vanishes.

assumptions_latex: The quadratic expression is \(q(x)=\tfrac12x^{\mathsf T}Qx+c^{\mathsf T}x+d\), with \(Q\) symmetric.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The expression has zero quadratic curvature exactly when \(Q=0\), in which case it is affine.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Identifies the zero-curvature member of the quadratic-function family.

source_refs.locator: Part I Convex Analysis

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A quadratic expression \(q(x)=\tfrac12x^{\mathsf T}Qx+c^{\mathsf T}x+d\), with \(Q=Q^{\mathsf T}\), is called affine-degenerate when \(Q=0\). Then \(q(x)=c^{\mathsf T}x+d\), its gradient is the constant vector \(c\), and its Hessian vanishes everywhere. Conversely, if a quadratic expression is affine on \(\mathbb R^n\), its Hessian is zero and therefore \(Q=0\). Such an expression is simultaneously convex and concave; its sublevel sets and superlevel sets are halfspaces, empty, or all of \(\mathbb R^n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A quadratic expression is actually affine exactly when its quadratic matrix is zero. It then has constant gradient, zero Hessian, and is both convex and concave.
knowledge_statements.title: Affine Quadratic Expressions

source_witnesses.locator: Part I Convex Analysis

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition and mathematical claims fit the leaf, but the locator "Part I Convex Analysis" is not a specific section, definition, theorem, or page locator as required. A precise source locator supporting the affine-degenerate quadratic characterization is needed.

children.title: Singular Curvature Quadratics
children.top_down_role: Quadratic expressions with singular curvature matrices.

assumptions_latex: The expression is \(q(x)=\tfrac12x^{\mathsf T}Qx+c^{\mathsf T}x+d\), with \(Q\succeq0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Singularity produces flat directions: curvature vanishes on \(\ker Q\), so the function is convex but not strictly convex on \(\mathbb R^n\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Treats nonzero singular positive-semidefinite curvature in convex quadratics.

source_refs.locator: 2.13 Convex Optimization p. 76

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Q\succeq0\) be nonzero and singular. Then \(q(x)=\tfrac12x^{\mathsf T}Qx+c^{\mathsf T}x+d\) is convex but not strictly convex on \(\mathbb R^n\). For every nonzero \(v\in\ker Q\), its restriction to a line parallel to \(v\) is \[q(x+tv)=q(x)+t c^{\mathsf T}v,\] so the quadratic curvature along that line is zero. If additionally \(c^{\mathsf T}v=0\), the function is constant along that direction. Hence singularity of \(Q\) distinguishes a convex quadratic with flat directions from a positive-definite, strictly convex quadratic.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonzero singular positive-semidefinite Hessian gives a convex but non-strictly-convex quadratic. Nullspace directions have zero quadratic curvature and may be completely flat.
knowledge_statements.title: Singular Curvature Quadratics

source_witnesses.locator: 2.13 Convex Optimization p. 76

children.title: Partially Curved Quadratics
children.top_down_role: Quadratic expressions containing both curved subspaces and flat directions.

assumptions_latex: The expression is \(q(x)=\tfrac12x^{\mathsf T}Qx+c^{\mathsf T}x+d\), with \(Q\succeq0\) and \(0<\operatorname{rank}Q<n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: After an orthogonal change of coordinates, the quadratic term depends only on the positive-curvature coordinates and vanishes on the complementary coordinates.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gives the spectral normal form separating curved and flat subspaces.

source_refs.locator: 4.1 Linear Equations in Optimization p. 55

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Q\in\mathbb S_+^n\) have rank \(r\), where \(0<r<n\). There is an orthogonal matrix \(U\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\) such that \[U^{\mathsf T}QU=\operatorname{diag}(\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_r,0,\ldots,0),\qquad \lambda_j>0\ \text{for }j=1,\ldots,r.\] For \(x\in\mathbb R^n\), write \(y=U^{\mathsf T}x\in\mathbb R^n\) and \(U^{\mathsf T}c=(a,b)\), where \(a\in\mathbb R^r\) and \(b\in\mathbb R^{n-r}\). Then \[q(Uy)=\tfrac12\sum_{j=1}^r\lambda_jy_j^2+a^{\mathsf T}y_{1:r}+b^{\mathsf T}y_{r+1:n}+d.\] Thus the expression is quadratically curved only on \(\operatorname{range}Q\); on \(\ker Q\) it is at most affine.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A rank-deficient positive-semidefinite quadratic splits orthogonally into positive-curvature coordinates and nullspace coordinates, with only affine dependence possible in the latter.
knowledge_statements.title: Partially Curved Quadratics

source_witnesses.locator: 4.1 Linear Equations in Optimization p. 55

assumptions_latex: The inequality reverses the standard convex-sublevel orientation and has the form \(q(x)\ge\alpha\), where \(q\) is convex and nonaffine.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A superlevel set of a convex quadratic need not be convex; therefore reversed convex quadratic inequalities fall outside general convex-QCQP recognition.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Shows why inequality orientation matters even when the quadratic function is convex.

source_refs.locator: 2.5 Convex Inequalities p. 52

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Convexity of \(q\) guarantees convexity of its sublevel sets, not of its superlevel sets. For the convex quadratic \(q(x)=x^2\) on \(\mathbb R\), the reversed inequality \(q(x)\ge1\) has feasible set \[S_1=(-\infty,-1]\cup[1,\infty),\] which is not convex because \(-1,1\in S_1\) while their midpoint \(0\notin S_1\). Hence rewriting a nonaffine convex quadratic constraint from \(q(x)\le\alpha\) to \(q(x)\ge\alpha\) destroys the general convexity guarantee. Special superlevel sets may be convex, but curvature alone does not establish that property.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Reversing a convex quadratic inequality generally destroys convexity. For example, the feasible set of x squared at least one is the union of two disjoint rays.
knowledge_statements.title: Reversed Convex Quadratic Inequalities

source_witnesses.locator: 2.5 Convex Inequalities p. 52

assumptions_latex: An equality constraint has the form \(q(x)=\alpha\), where \(q\) is a nonaffine convex quadratic.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A nonaffine quadratic equality does not generally define a convex feasible set and therefore is excluded from the standard convex-QCQP class.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Explains the affine-equality restriction in standard convex optimization models.

source_refs.locator: 2.13 Convex Optimization p. 76

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A quadratic equality \(q(x)=\alpha\) is the intersection of \(q(x)\le\alpha\) and \(q(x)\ge\alpha\); the second constraint has the reversed convex orientation when \(q\) is convex. Concretely, for \(q(x)=x^2\) and \(\alpha=1\), the level set is \[L_1=\{-1,1\},\] which is not convex. Thus a nonaffine quadratic equality is not a valid convex constraint in general. If the quadratic term vanishes, the equality is affine and its feasible set is an affine subspace; exceptional nonaffine equalities may be convex only through degeneracy, such as an empty or singleton level set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonaffine quadratic equality generally gives a nonconvex level set; x squared equals one yields two points. Standard convex QCQPs therefore permit only affine equalities.
knowledge_statements.title: Nonaffine Quadratic Equalities

source_witnesses.locator: 2.13 Convex Optimization p. 76

assumptions_latex: The symmetric matrix \(Q\succeq0\) admits a factorization \(Q=R^{\mathsf T}R\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The quadratic inequality is equivalent to a second-order-cone norm inequality, provided the affine right-hand side is constrained to be nonnegative.

notation.meaning: matrix factor satisfying Q equals R transpose R

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Represents positive-semidefinite quadratic forms through Euclidean norms and the Lorentz cone.

source_refs.locator: 2.5 Convex Inequalities p. 52

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Q=R^{\mathsf T}R\succeq0\), let \(a\in\mathbb R^n\), and let \(b\in\mathbb R\). Then \[x^{\mathsf T}Qx\le(a^{\mathsf T}x+b)^2,\qquad a^{\mathsf T}x+b\ge0,\] is equivalent to \[\|Rx\|_2\le a^{\mathsf T}x+b,\] or, equivalently, \((a^{\mathsf T}x+b,Rx)\in\mathcal Q^{k+1}\), where \(R\) has \(k\) rows. The explicit sign condition is essential because squaring alone loses the sign of the affine right-hand side. The special epigraph constraint \(x^{\mathsf T}Qx\le t^2\), \(t\ge0\), is therefore second-order-cone representable as \(\|Rx\|_2\le t\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Factoring a positive-semidefinite quadratic as a squared Euclidean norm converts its comparison with a nonnegative affine square into a Lorentz-cone constraint.
knowledge_statements.title: Factored-Norm Representations

source_witnesses.locator: 2.5 Convex Inequalities p. 52

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A product-bounded squared norm is exactly a rotated-cone membership constraint.

knowledge_statements.title: Dual-Function Geometry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Geometry and closed-form evaluation of the QCQP Lagrangian dual function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define
\[
H(\lambda)=Q_0+\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_iQ_i,\quad
h(\lambda)=q_0+\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_iq_i,\quad
c(\lambda)=r_0+\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_ir_i.
\]
For \(\lambda\in\mathbb R_+^m\), the dual function \(g(\lambda)=\inf_{x\in\mathbb R^n}L(x,\lambda)\) is concave and satisfies
\[
g(\lambda)=
\begin{cases}
c(\lambda)-h(\lambda)^{\mathsf T}H(\lambda)^\dagger h(\lambda),&H(\lambda)\succeq0\text{ and }h(\lambda)\in\operatorname{Range}(H(\lambda)),\\
-\infty,&\text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The QCQP dual function is concave; it is finite exactly when the aggregated Hessian is positive semidefinite and the aggregated linear term lies in its range.
assumptions_latex: \(f_i(x)=x^{\mathsf T}Q_i x+2q_i^{\mathsf T}x+r_i\) for \(i=0,\ldots,m\), where \(x\in\mathbb R^n\), \(Q_i\in\mathbb S^n\), \(q_i\in\mathbb R^n\), and \(r_i\in\mathbb R\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The dual function is concave, with the displayed effective domain and value formula.

notation.meaning: Aggregated quadratic, linear, and constant coefficients of the Lagrangian.

knowledge_statements.title: Weak-Duality Bounds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Weak Lagrangian duality for inequality-constrained QCQP.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let
\[
p^*=\inf\{f_0(x):x\in\mathbb R^n,\ f_i(x)\le0,\ i=1,\ldots,m\}
\]
and
\[
g(\lambda)=\inf_{x\in\mathbb R^n}\left(f_0(x)+\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i f_i(x)\right),\qquad \lambda\in\mathbb R_+^m.
\]
Then
\[
g(\lambda)\le p^*\qquad\text{for every }\lambda\in\mathbb R_+^m,
\]
and, for \(d^*=\sup_{\lambda\in\mathbb R_+^m}g(\lambda)\),
\[
d^*\le p^*.
\]
These bounds require neither convexity nor a constraint qualification, with consistent extended-real conventions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every nonnegative multiplier produces a valid lower bound on the primal QCQP value, so the dual value never exceeds the primal value.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every \(\lambda\in\mathbb R_+^m\), \(g(\lambda)\le p^*\), and hence \(d^*\le p^*\).

notation.meaning: Dual optimal value, the supremum of g over nonnegative multipliers.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
When strict feasibility fails, weak duality \(d^*\le p^*\) remains valid, but Slater's theorem alone yields neither equality nor dual attainment. For the convex QCQP
\[
\min_{x\in\mathbb R}\ x^2\quad\text{subject to}\quad (x-1)^2\le0,
\]
the unique feasible point is \(x=1\), so \(p^*=1\). Its dual function is
\[
g(\lambda)=\inf_x\bigl(x^2+\lambda(x-1)^2\bigr)=\frac{\lambda}{1+\lambda},\qquad \lambda\ge0.
\]
Hence \(d^*=1=p^*\), but no finite multiplier attains \(d^*\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Without strict feasibility, weak duality survives but strong-duality guarantees do not; a boundary-only convex QCQP can already lose dual attainment.

\[
f_i(\bar x)<0\qquad\text{for every }i=1,\ldots,m.
