knowledge_statements.title: Constraint Degeneracy Mechanisms
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Mechanisms preventing strict feasibility in a conic representation of a convex QCQP.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let the lifted feasible set be \(F=\{z\in K:Az=b\}\), where \(K\) is a closed convex cone. Constraint degeneracy occurs whenever \(F\neq\varnothing\) but \(F\cap\operatorname{ri}K=\varnothing\). Equivalently, the affine constraints force every feasible lift into a proper face of \(K\). Typical mechanisms are an equality implied by active quadratic inequalities, a positive-semidefinite block forced to have a common null vector, or a Lorentz-cone block forced onto its boundary. In each case Slater's condition fails despite feasibility, so ordinary constraint qualifications and attainment of dual multipliers are not guaranteed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Degeneracy arises when affine and quadratic constraints force every feasible conic lift into a proper cone face, eliminating strict feasibility and potentially disrupting dual attainment or multiplier existence.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\cap\operatorname{ri}K=\varnothing\), equivalently \(F\) lies in a proper face of \(K\).

knowledge_statements.title: Minimal-Face Geometry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minimal-face reformulation of a feasible conic lift of a convex QCQP.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a nonempty lifted feasible set \(F=\{z\in K:Az=b\}\), define \(K_{\min}=\operatorname{face}_K(F)\), the intersection of all faces of \(K\) containing \(F\). Then \(K_{\min}\) is the unique minimal face containing every feasible lift, and \(F\cap\operatorname{ri}K_{\min}\neq\varnothing\). Replacing \(z\in K\) by \(z\in K_{\min}\) preserves the feasible set and objective values while restoring relative strict feasibility. Thus boundary-only feasibility in \(K\) becomes strict feasibility relative to the reduced cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every nonempty conic lift has a unique smallest containing face; restricting the model to it preserves feasibility and restores relative strict feasibility.

knowledge_statements.title: Facial-Reduction Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary between direct Slater duality and facially reduced conic duality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider a feasible conic representation \(F=\{z\in K:Az=b\}\) of a convex QCQP. Facial reduction is unnecessary exactly when \(F\cap\operatorname{ri}K\neq\varnothing\). If instead \(F\neq\varnothing\) and \(F\cap\operatorname{ri}K=\varnothing\), the model lies beyond the direct-Slater boundary: every feasible point belongs to a proper face \(K_{\min}\subsetneq K\). Duality results requiring strict feasibility must then be applied after replacing \(K\) by \(K_{\min}\), or after an equivalent facial-reduction sequence identifies that face.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Facial reduction becomes necessary precisely when a feasible conic QCQP lift has no point in the cone's relative interior and therefore occupies a proper face.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\cap\operatorname{ri}K=\varnothing\) implies \(\operatorname{face}_K(F)\subsetneq K\).

knowledge_statements.title: Primal-Dual Solution Geometry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Geometric structure of KKT pairs for differentiable convex QCQPs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f_i(x)=\tfrac12x^{\mathsf T}Q_i x+q_i^{\mathsf T}x+r_i\) with \(Q_i\succeq0\) for \(i=0,\ldots,m\), and impose \(f_i(x)\leq0\) for \(i\geq1\). The primal-dual solution set consists of pairs \((x,\lambda)\) satisfying primal feasibility, \(\lambda\geq0\), stationarity \(\nabla f_0(x)+\sum_i\lambda_i\nabla f_i(x)=0\), and complementarity \(\lambda_i f_i(x)=0\). For fixed \(\lambda\), primal solutions minimize the convex quadratic Lagrangian; positive multipliers can occur only on active constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Primal-dual solutions are exactly feasible, stationary, complementary pairs; each fixed multiplier exposes the minimizer set of a convex quadratic Lagrangian.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((x,\lambda)\) obeys feasibility, stationarity, complementarity, and \(\lambda_i>0\Rightarrow f_i(x)=0\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard KKT geometry for differentiable convex programs
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The property describes KKT-pair geometry for a convex inequality-only QCQP, but no source supports the exact characterization or its relation to the full primal-dual solution set.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Positive Active-Gradient Representation and Strict Complementarity of SDP-QCQP
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalence at a unique QCQP optimum between a strictly positive active-gradient representation and a strictly complementary optimum of the SDP-QCQP dual.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose \(y\) is the unique optimal solution of \((QCQP)\), and hence is also optimal for \((SDP\text{-}QCQP)\) with the associated slacks \(\bar z^1,\ldots,\bar z^m\). Suppose constraints \(1,\ldots,k\) are exactly the tight QCQP constraints at \(y\). Then \(b\) is a strictly positive combination of the gradients of those tight constraints if and only if the dual of \((SDP\text{-}QCQP)\) has an optimal solution strictly complementary to \((\bar y,\bar z^1,\ldots,\bar z^m)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a unique QCQP optimum that is also optimal for its SDP formulation, the objective vector is a strictly positive combination of all active-constraint gradients exactly when the SDP dual has an optimum strictly complementary to the associated primal point and slacks.
assumptions_latex: y\text{ is the unique optimal solution of }(QCQP)
y\text{ is also optimal for }(SDP\text{-}QCQP)\text{ with associated slacks }\bar z^1,\ldots,\bar z^m
\{1,\ldots,k\}\text{ is exactly the set of tight QCQP constraints at }y
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: b\text{ is a strictly positive combination of the gradients of constraints }1,\ldots,k\iff\exists\text{ an optimal dual solution of }(SDP\text{-}QCQP)\text{ strictly complementary to }(\bar y,\bar z^1,\ldots,\bar z^m).

knowledge_statements.title: KKT Global-Optimality Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sufficient KKT certificate for global optimality of a convex QCQP.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f_i(x)=\tfrac12x^{\mathsf T}Q_i x+q_i^{\mathsf T}x+r_i\), where \(Q_i\succeq0\) for \(i=0,\ldots,m\). A pair \((x^\star,\lambda^\star)\) certifies global optimality if \(f_i(x^\star)\leq0\), \(\lambda_i^\star\geq0\), \(\lambda_i^\star f_i(x^\star)=0\) for \(i=1,\ldots,m\), and \(\nabla f_0(x^\star)+\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i^\star\nabla f_i(x^\star)=0\). Under these conditions, \(x^\star\) is a global minimizer of the convex QCQP.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a convex inequality-only QCQP, primal feasibility, nonnegative multipliers, stationarity, and complementarity certify global optimality.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f_0(x^\star)\leq f_0(x)\) for every feasible \(x\).

knowledge_statements.title: Multiplier-Based Value Sensitivity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: First-order value sensitivity to right-hand-side perturbations of convex quadratic constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(v(u)=\inf\{f_0(x):f_i(x)\leq u_i,\ i=1,\ldots,m\}\). Suppose the unperturbed convex QCQP satisfies Slater's condition, has finite value, and admits an optimal multiplier \(\lambda^\star\). Then \(-\lambda^\star\in\partial v(0)\), so \(v(u)\geq v(0)-\langle\lambda^\star,u\rangle\) for every perturbation \(u\) in the effective domain. If \(v\) is differentiable at \(0\), its gradient is unique and satisfies \(\nabla v(0)=-\lambda^\star\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Optimal multipliers give subgradients of the perturbed optimal value; under differentiability, the value gradient is the negative multiplier vector.
assumptions_latex: The QCQP is convex and has finite value at \(u=0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(-\lambda^\star\in\partial v(0)\), and differentiability gives \(\nabla v(0)=-\lambda^\star\).

knowledge_statements.title: Solution-Map Stability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local single-valued Lipschitz stability under strong regularity of the QCQP KKT system.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a parametrized convex QCQP have twice continuously differentiable data near a KKT point \((x^\star,\lambda^\star)\). If LICQ holds for the active constraints, strict complementarity holds, and the Lagrangian Hessian is positive definite on the critical tangent space, then sufficiently small parameter perturbations admit a unique nearby KKT pair \((x(p),\lambda(p))\). The mapping \(p\mapsto(x(p),\lambda(p))\) is locally Lipschitz; when the active set and data vary smoothly, it is continuously differentiable. Consequently the local primal solution is unique and stable against small coefficient and right-hand-side perturbations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: LICQ, strict complementarity, and second-order positivity make the nearby primal-dual solution unique and locally Lipschitz under small QCQP perturbations.
assumptions_latex: The parametrized QCQP data are twice continuously differentiable.
LICQ and strict complementarity hold at \((x^\star,\lambda^\star)\).
The Lagrangian Hessian is positive definite on the critical tangent space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There is a unique nearby KKT mapping \(p\mapsto(x(p),\lambda(p))\), locally Lipschitz at the reference parameter.

knowledge_statements.title: SOCP Interface
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Second-order-cone epigraph representation of positive-semidefinite quadratic functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Q=A^{\mathsf T}A\succeq0\). The convex quadratic inequality \(x^{\mathsf T}Qx+q^{\mathsf T}x+r\leq0\) is equivalent to introducing \(t=-q^{\mathsf T}x-r\) and imposing \(t\geq0\) together with \((t/2,1,Ax)\in\mathcal Q_r\), where \(\mathcal Q_r=\{(u,v,w):2uv\geq\|w\|_2^2,\ u\geq0,\ v\geq0\}\). Applying this construction to each convex quadratic constraint, and to an objective epigraph, yields an SOCP with the same feasible points and optimal value.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Factoring each positive-semidefinite quadratic converts its epigraph inequality into one rotated second-order-cone constraint, producing an equivalent SOCP.
assumptions_latex: The scalar quadratic inequality is convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x^{\mathsf T}Qx+q^{\mathsf T}x+r\leq0\iff t=-q^{\mathsf T}x-r\geq0\) and \((t/2,1,Ax)\in\mathcal Q_r\).

knowledge_statements.title: SDP Interface
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Schur-complement semidefinite representation of positive-semidefinite quadratic inequalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x\in\mathbb R^n\), let \(Q=A^{\mathsf T}A\succeq0\), and let \(I\) be the identity matrix whose order equals the row dimension of \(A\). The inequality \(x^{\mathsf T}Qx+q^{\mathsf T}x+r\leq0\) is equivalent to the linear matrix inequality \[\begin{pmatrix}-q^{\mathsf T}x-r&(Ax)^{\mathsf T}\\Ax&I\end{pmatrix}\succeq0.\] Applying this representation to every convex quadratic constraint and to an objective epigraph produces an SDP with identical feasible projections and optimal value.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A positive-semidefinite quadratic inequality is equivalent to a block linear matrix inequality, yielding an SDP formulation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x^{\mathsf T}Qx+q^{\mathsf T}x+r\leq0\iff \begin{pmatrix}-q^{\mathsf T}x-r&(Ax)^{\mathsf T}\\Ax&I\end{pmatrix}\succeq0\).

knowledge_statements.title: Conic Representation Size
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dimension counts for direct SOCP and SDP representations of convex QCQP constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(m\) inequalities with \(Q_i=A_i^{\mathsf T}A_i\) and \(r_i=\operatorname{rank}Q_i\), the direct rotated-SOCP formulation uses one cone block of dimension \(r_i+2\) per inequality and only affine auxiliary slacks. Its total cone dimension is \(\sum_{i=1}^m(r_i+2)\). The direct Schur-complement SDP formulation uses one positive-semidefinite block of order \(r_i+1\) per inequality, containing \((r_i+1)(r_i+2)/2\) scalar matrix entries. These are formulation-size counts, not iteration-complexity bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Rank-factorized SOCP blocks grow linearly with quadratic rank, whereas direct SDP blocks contain quadratically many scalar matrix entries.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The SOCP cone dimension is \(\sum_i(r_i+2)\); SDP block \(i\) has order \(r_i+1\) and \((r_i+1)(r_i+2)/2\) scalar entries.

knowledge_statements.title: Representation Sparsity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Preservation and loss of sparsity in conic representations of convex quadratic forms.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(Q=A^{\mathsf T}A\succeq0\), both the SOCP and Schur-complement SDP interfaces depend on the factor product \(Ax\). Their explicit linear-operator sparsity is therefore governed by \(A\), not solely by the sparsity pattern of \(Q\). A dense square-root factor can destroy sparsity even when \(Q\) is sparse. If a sparse factorization or chordal decomposition is available, separate smaller cone or semidefinite blocks may preserve locality, subject to consistency constraints on shared variables or clique overlaps.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Conic-form sparsity depends on the chosen quadratic factorization; dense factors can erase sparse structure, while sparse or chordal decompositions can preserve locality.
assumptions_latex: The conic representation is built from \(Ax\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The operator sparsity of the conic lift follows the sparsity of \(A\), and need not equal the sparsity of \(Q\).

knowledge_statements.title: Numerical Scaling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Positive diagonal variable and constraint scaling for a finite-dimensional convex QCQP.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For quadratic constraints \(q_i(x)=\tfrac12 x^{\mathsf T}Q_i x+a_i^{\mathsf T}x-b_i\le 0\), choose a positive diagonal matrix \(D\) and positive scalars \(s_i\). Under \(x=Dz\), the equivalent scaled constraints are \(\widehat q_i(z)=s_iq_i(Dz)\le0\), with \(\widehat Q_i=s_iD^{\mathsf T}Q_iD\), \(\widehat a_i=s_iD^{\mathsf T}a_i\), and \(\widehat b_i=s_ib_i\). The map \(z\mapsto Dz\) is a bijection between the scaled and original feasible sets. Congruence preserves positive semidefiniteness, so convexity is unchanged, although coefficient norms and numerical conditioning may change.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Positive diagonal changes of variables and positive constraint rescaling preserve feasibility and convexity while changing coefficient magnitudes and potentially numerical conditioning.
assumptions_latex: \(D\) is diagonal with strictly positive diagonal entries.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(q_i(Dz)\le0\iff \widehat q_i(z)\le0\), and \(Q_i\succeq0\iff \widehat Q_i\succeq0\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: positive diagonal substitutions and positive inequality scaling give the displayed algebraic equivalence

knowledge_statements.title: Tangent-Cone Geometry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bouligand tangent cone of a QCQP feasible set at a feasible point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(F=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:q_i(x)\le0\ (i=1,\ldots,m),\ h_j(x)=0\ (j=1,\ldots,p)\}\) and \(\bar x\in F\). The Bouligand tangent cone is
\[T_F(\bar x)=\left\{d\in\mathbb R^n:\exists\,t_k\downarrow0,\ d_k\to d\text{ with }\bar x+t_kd_k\in F\text{ for every }k\right\}.\]
It is a closed cone and records precisely the first-order velocities of feasible sequences, including velocities not detected exactly by linearizing degenerate active constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The tangent cone consists of limits of directions along feasible sequences approaching the reference feasible point.
assumptions_latex: \(q_i\) and \(h_j\) are quadratic functions on \(\mathbb R^n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T_F(\bar x)\) is a closed cone of feasible first-order velocities.

notation.meaning: Bouligand tangent cone at the feasible point

knowledge_statements.title: Linearized-Cone Geometry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: First-order cone obtained by linearizing active QCQP constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For the feasible set \(F\) and \(\bar x\in F\), let \(I(\bar x)=\{i:q_i(\bar x)=0\}\). The linearized cone is
\[L_F(\bar x)=\left\{d\in\mathbb R^n:\nabla q_i(\bar x)^{\mathsf T}d\le0\ \text{for }i\in I(\bar x),\quad \nabla h_j(\bar x)^{\mathsf T}d=0\ \text{for }j=1,\ldots,p\right\}.\]
This is a closed convex polyhedral cone determined solely by the active gradients. Every tangent direction satisfies the linearized relations, hence \(T_F(\bar x)\subseteq L_F(\bar x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The linearized cone imposes first-order inequalities for active constraints and first-order equalities for equality constraints; it always contains the tangent cone.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T_F(\bar x)\subseteq L_F(\bar x)\), and \(L_F(\bar x)\) is closed, convex, and polyhedral.

notation.meaning: linearized cone at the feasible point

knowledge_statements.title: Cone-Coincidence Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Tangent and linearized cones coincide under Mangasarian–Fromovitz regularity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(F\) be defined by continuously differentiable inequalities \(q_i(x)\le0\) and equalities \(h_j(x)=0\), and let \(\bar x\in F\). Suppose the equality gradients are linearly independent and there exists \(w\in\mathbb R^n\) such that \(\nabla h_j(\bar x)^{\mathsf T}w=0\) for every \(j\) and \(\nabla q_i(\bar x)^{\mathsf T}w<0\) for every \(i\in I(\bar x)\). Then the feasible set is first-order regular at \(\bar x\) and
\[T_F(\bar x)=L_F(\bar x).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under MFCQ, every direction satisfying the linearized active constraints is realizable as a tangent direction, so the two cones coincide.
assumptions_latex: The constraint functions are continuously differentiable near \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T_F(\bar x)=L_F(\bar x)\).

knowledge_statements.title: Normal-Cone Geometry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Regular and limiting normal cones of a QCQP feasible set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a closed feasible set \(F\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) and \(\bar x\in F\), the regular normal cone is
\[\widehat N_F(\bar x)=T_F(\bar x)^\circ=\{v:v^{\mathsf T}d\le0\text{ for every }d\in T_F(\bar x)\}.\]
The limiting normal cone is
\[N_F(\bar x)=\{v:\exists\,x_k\to\bar x,\ x_k\in F,\ v_k\to v,\ v_k\in\widehat N_F(x_k)\}.\]
Always \(\widehat N_F(\bar x)\subseteq N_F(\bar x)\); the regular cone is closed and convex, whereas the limiting cone need not be convex without regularity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Regular normals polarize tangent directions; limiting normals are limits of nearby regular normals and may form a larger, nonconvex cone.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\widehat N_F(\bar x)=T_F(\bar x)^\circ\subseteq N_F(\bar x)\).

knowledge_statements.title: Multiplier-Set Geometry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Geometry of multipliers representing a prescribed normal vector at a feasible point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(v\in\mathbb R^n\) and feasible \(\bar x\), define
\[\Lambda(\bar x,v)=\left\{(\lambda,\mu):v=\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i\nabla q_i(\bar x)+\sum_{j=1}^p\mu_j\nabla h_j(\bar x),\ \lambda_i\ge0,\ \lambda_iq_i(\bar x)=0\right\}.\]
Because the gradients are fixed at \(\bar x\), this set is a possibly empty, unbounded, closed convex polyhedron. If the active inequality gradients together with the equality gradients are linearly independent, then \(\Lambda(\bar x,v)\) contains at most one multiplier pair.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Multipliers representing a fixed normal form a closed convex polyhedron; under LICQ the representation, when it exists, is unique.
assumptions_latex: The QCQP constraints are differentiable at \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\Lambda(\bar x,v)\) is polyhedral, and LICQ implies \(|\Lambda(\bar x,v)|\le1\).

knowledge_statements.title: Normal-Multiplier Correspondence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gradient representation of QCQP normals under Mangasarian–Fromovitz regularity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(F\) be defined by continuously differentiable inequalities \(q_i(x)\le0\) and equalities \(h_j(x)=0\), and suppose MFCQ holds at \(\bar x\in F\). Then \(F\) is normally regular at \(\bar x\), and
\[\widehat N_F(\bar x)=N_F(\bar x)=\left\{\sum_{i\in I(\bar x)}\lambda_i\nabla q_i(\bar x)+\sum_{j=1}^p\mu_j\nabla h_j(\bar x):\lambda_i\ge0,\ \mu_j\in\mathbb R\right\}.\]
Equivalently, a vector \(v\) is normal to \(F\) at \(\bar x\) exactly when \(\Lambda(\bar x,v)\) is nonempty.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under MFCQ, regular and limiting normals coincide and are exactly the conic-linear combinations represented by feasible multipliers.
assumptions_latex: The constraint functions are continuously differentiable near \(\bar x\).

knowledge_statements.title: QCQP Critical Cones
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Critical directions for a differentiable QCQP at a KKT point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(F=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:q_i(x)\le 0\ (i=1,\ldots,m),\ h_j(x)=0\ (j=1,\ldots,p)\}\), and consider minimizing \(f(x)\) over \(F\). Let \( ar x\in F\) admit KKT multipliers \((\lambda,\mu)\) satisfying \(
abla f( ar x)+\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i
abla q_i( ar x)+\sum_{j=1}^p\mu_j
abla h_j( ar x)=0\), \(\lambda_i\ge0\), and \(\lambda_iq_i( ar x)=0\). The critical cone is
\[\mathcal C( ar x)=\{d\in L_F( ar x):
abla f( ar x)^{\mathsf T}d=0\}.\]
Equivalently, \(d\in\mathcal C( ar x)\) exactly when \(
abla h_j( ar x)^{\mathsf T}d=0\) for every \(j\), \(
abla q_i( ar x)^{\mathsf T}d=0\) for every active \(i\) with \(\lambda_i>0\), and \(
abla q_i( ar x)^{\mathsf T}d\le0\) for every active \(i\) with \(\lambda_i=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a KKT point, the critical cone consists of linearized feasible directions having zero first-order objective change; positive inequality multipliers identify active constraints that must remain tangent.
assumptions_latex: A KKT multiplier pair \((\lambda,\mu)\) exists with the displayed stationarity sign convention.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal C(\bar x)=L_F(\bar x)\cap\{d\in\mathbb R^n:\nabla f(\bar x)^{\mathsf T}d=0\}\).

notation.meaning: critical cone at the KKT point

knowledge_statements.title: Linear-Independence Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Linear independence constraint qualification for active QCQP constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a feasible point \(\bar x\), LICQ holds when the family
\[\{\nabla q_i(\bar x):i\in I(\bar x)\}\cup\{\nabla h_j(\bar x):j=1,\ldots,p\}\]
is linearly independent. Equivalently, the only coefficients satisfying
\[\sum_{i\in I(\bar x)}\alpha_i\nabla q_i(\bar x)+\sum_{j=1}^p\beta_j\nabla h_j(\bar x)=0\]
are \(\alpha_i=0\) and \(\beta_j=0\). LICQ implies MFCQ and makes every multiplier representation associated with a fixed stationarity or normal vector unique.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: LICQ requires all active inequality gradients and equality gradients to be linearly independent; it implies MFCQ and uniqueness of any existing multipliers.
assumptions_latex: All QCQP constraints are differentiable at \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{rank}[\nabla q_i(\bar x)_{i\in I(\bar x)},\nabla h_j(\bar x)_{j=1}^p]=|I(\bar x)|+p\).

notation.meaning: coefficients in an active-gradient dependence relation

knowledge_statements.title: Mangasarian-Fromovitz Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Mangasarian–Fromovitz constraint qualification for active QCQP constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(I( ar x)=\{i:q_i( ar x)=0\}\) at a feasible point \( ar x\). MFCQ holds at \( ar x\) if the equality gradients \(
abla h_1( ar x),\ldots,
abla h_p( ar x)\) are linearly independent and there exists \(w\in\mathbb R^n\) satisfying
\[
abla h_j( ar x)^{\mathsf T}w=0\quad(j=1,\ldots,p),\qquad 
abla q_i( ar x)^{\mathsf T}w<0\quad(i\in I( ar x)).\]
Thus one first-order direction preserves every equality while strictly entering every active inequality. LICQ implies MFCQ, while MFCQ permits linearly dependent active inequality gradients.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: MFCQ requires linearly independent equality gradients and a direction tangent to every equality that strictly decreases every active inequality.
assumptions_latex: All QCQP constraints are differentiable at \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex:
\(\{
abla h_j( ar x):j=1,\ldots,p\}\) is linearly independent and \(\exists w\in\mathbb R^n\) such that \(
abla h_j( ar x)^{\mathsf T}w=0\) for every \(j\) and \(
abla q_i( ar x)^{\mathsf T}w<0\) for every \(i\in I( ar x)\).

knowledge_statements.title: Weaker Constraint Qualifications
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Abadie and Guignard cone conditions at a feasible QCQP point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
At \(\bar x\in F\), the Abadie constraint qualification is
\[T_F(\bar x)=L_F(\bar x),\]
whereas the Guignard constraint qualification is
\[T_F(\bar x)^\circ=L_F(\bar x)^\circ.\]
Because \(T_F(\bar x)\subseteq L_F(\bar x)\), Abadie implies Guignard. For continuously differentiable constraints, MFCQ implies Abadie, but neither displayed converse holds in general. Guignard is sufficient for replacing tangent-cone polars by linearized-cone polars in first-order normal and multiplier conditions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Abadie equates tangent and linearized cones; Guignard only equates their polars. MFCQ implies Abadie, which implies Guignard.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) is defined by continuously differentiable constraints near \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathrm{MFCQ}\Rightarrow\mathrm{ACQ}\Rightarrow\mathrm{GCQ}\), with converses failing in general.

knowledge_statements.title: Constant-Rank Constraint Qualifications
knowledge_statements.scope_note: CRCQ for active inequality and equality gradients near a feasible QCQP point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(I(\bar x)=\{i:q_i(\bar x)=0\}\). CRCQ holds at \(\bar x\) if there exists a neighborhood \(U\) of \(\bar x\) such that, for every subset \(J\subseteq I(\bar x)\), the rank of
\[\{\nabla q_i(x):i\in J\}\cup\{\nabla h_j(x):j=1,\ldots,p\}\]
is constant for all \(x\in U\). The condition allows dependence among active gradients but forbids the rank of any selected active-gradient family from changing locally. LICQ implies CRCQ; the converse need not hold.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: CRCQ requires every selected family of active inequality gradients, together with all equality gradients, to retain constant rank near the feasible point.
assumptions_latex: The QCQP constraints are continuously differentiable near \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{rank}(\{\nabla q_i(x):i\in J\}\cup\{\nabla h_j(x):1\le j\le p\})\) is locally constant for every \(J\subseteq I(\bar x)\).

At a feasible point \( ar x\), MFCQ is equivalent to the nonexistence of \((\lambda,\mu)
eq(0,0)\) satisfying \(\mu_j\geq0\) for every \(j\in A( ar x)\) and \[\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i
abla h_i( ar x)+\sum_{j\in A( ar x)}\mu_j
abla g_j( ar x)=0.\] Hence, if MFCQ holds, every Fritz John multiplier tuple \((\alpha,\lambda,\mu)\) at \( ar x\) has \(\alpha>0\) and division by \(\alpha\) yields a KKT multiplier tuple. children.top_down_role: Singular or rank-deficient second-order structure at stationary points.

knowledge_statements.title: Lagrangian Hessian Degeneracy
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Degeneracy on the QCQP critical cone at a KKT point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Consider a QCQP with quadratic objective \(f\), inequality constraints \(g_i\le 0\), equality constraints \(h_j=0\), and Lagrangian \(L(x,\lambda,
u)=f(x)+\sum_i\lambda_i g_i(x)+\sum_j
u_jh_j(x)\). At a KKT triple \(( ar x, ar\lambda, ar
u)\), let \(C( ar x, ar\lambda)\) be its critical cone and let \(H=
abla^2_{xx}L( ar x, ar\lambda, ar
u)\). The Lagrangian Hessian is degenerate on the critical cone precisely when there exists \(d\in C( ar x, ar\lambda)\setminus\{0\}\) such that \(d^{\mathsf T}Hd=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Degeneracy occurs when a nonzero critical direction has zero quadratic curvature under the Lagrangian Hessian.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(H\text{ is critical-cone degenerate}\iff\exists d\in C(\bar x,\bar\lambda)\setminus\{0\}:d^{\mathsf T}Hd=0.\)

notation.meaning: Lagrangian Hessian at the KKT triple

children.title: Second-Order Inconclusive Regimes
children.top_down_role: Cases where available second-order curvature does not classify local behavior.

knowledge_statements.title: Second-Order Inconclusive Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary where necessary curvature holds but strict second-order sufficiency fails.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((\bar x,\bar\lambda,\bar\nu)\) be a KKT triple of a QCQP, with critical cone \(C\) and Lagrangian Hessian \(H\). A second-order inconclusive regime occurs when \(d^{\mathsf T}Hd\ge 0\) for every \(d\in C\), while \(d_0^{\mathsf T}Hd_0=0\) for some \(d_0\in C\setminus\{0\}\). Thus the second-order necessary condition holds, but positive definiteness on nonzero critical directions fails. These tests alone certify neither that \(\bar x\) is a strict local minimizer nor that it is not a local minimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Nonnegative critical curvature with at least one zero-curvature direction satisfies necessity but leaves local minimality unresolved.
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is the associated critical cone and \(H=\nabla^2_{xx}L(\bar x,\bar\lambda,\bar\nu)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(H\succeq_C0\) and \(\exists d_0\in C\setminus\{0\}:d_0^{\mathsf T}Hd_0=0\), so strict second-order sufficiency is unavailable.

notation.meaning: critical cone at the KKT point

children.title: Strict Local Minima
children.top_down_role: Local minimizers with strict objective separation from nearby feasible points.

knowledge_statements.title: Strict Local Minima
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strict feasible local minimality for a finite-dimensional QCQP.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be the feasible set of a QCQP with objective \(f\). A point \(\bar x\in F\) is a strict local minimizer if there exists \(r>0\) such that \(f(x)>f(\bar x)\) for every \(x\in F\cap B_r(\bar x)\) with \(x\ne\bar x\). The definition compares only feasible points and does not require \(\bar x\) to be globally optimal.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A strict local minimizer has strictly smaller objective than every other sufficiently close feasible point.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) is the QCQP feasible set and \(f:F\to\mathbb R\) is its objective.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\bar x\text{ is strict local}\iff\exists r>0\;\forall x\in F\cap B_r(\bar x)\setminus\{\bar x\},\ f(x)>f(\bar x).\)

children.title: Nonstrict Local Minima
children.top_down_role: Local minimizers permitting nearby feasible points with equal objective value.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonstrict Local Minima
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local minimality with arbitrarily nearby equal-value feasible points.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be the feasible set of a QCQP with objective \(f\). A point \(\bar x\in F\) is a nonstrict local minimizer if some \(r>0\) satisfies \(f(x)\ge f(\bar x)\) for every \(x\in F\cap B_r(\bar x)\), but \(\bar x\) is not strict. Equivalently, every \(\varepsilon>0\) admits \(x_\varepsilon\in F\setminus\{\bar x\}\) with \(\lVert x_\varepsilon-\bar x\rVert<\varepsilon\) and \(f(x_\varepsilon)=f(\bar x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonstrict local minimizer has no better nearby feasible point but has distinct equal-value feasible points arbitrarily close.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) is the QCQP feasible set and \(f:F\to\mathbb R\) is continuous.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\bar x\text{ is nonstrict local}\iff\bar x\text{ is local and }\forall\varepsilon>0\;\exists x_\varepsilon\ne\bar x:\ x_\varepsilon\in F,\ \lVert x_\varepsilon-\bar x\rVert<\varepsilon,\ f(x_\varepsilon)=f(\bar x).\)

children.title: Strictness Transition Regimes
children.top_down_role: Structural changes that separate strict from nonstrict local minimality.

knowledge_statements.title: Strictness Transition Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Parameter values at which a branch of strict local minima becomes nonstrict.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider a parameterized family of QCQPs with feasible sets \(F_\theta\), objectives \(f_\theta\), and a continuous feasible branch \(x(\theta)\). A parameter \(\theta_*\) is a strictness-transition value along this branch if there is a sequence \(\theta_k\to\theta_*\) such that each \(x(\theta_k)\) is a strict local minimizer, whereas \(x(\theta_*)\) is a nonstrict local minimizer. Hence distinct points of \(F_{\theta_*}\) having objective value \(f_{\theta_*}(x(\theta_*))\) accumulate at \(x(\theta_*)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strictness transitions when strict local minima approach a parameter value whose limiting local minimizer has nearby equal-value feasible points.
assumptions_latex: Each \(f_\theta\) and every constraint defining \(F_\theta\) is quadratic in the decision variable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\theta_k\to\theta_*,\ x(\theta_k)\text{ strict local},\quad x(\theta_*)\text{ nonstrict local}.\)

children.title: QCQP Saddle Points
children.top_down_role: Stationary feasible points exhibiting locally mixed landscape behavior.

knowledge_statements.title: QCQP Saddle Points
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Constrained saddle behavior defined through feasible objective variation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be the feasible set of a QCQP with objective \(f\). A feasible point \(\bar x\in F\) is a QCQP saddle point if, for every \(r>0\), there exist \(x_r^-,x_r^+\in F\cap B_r(\bar x)\) such that \(f(x_r^-)<f(\bar x)<f(x_r^+)\). Thus arbitrarily small feasible neighborhoods contain both descent and ascent points, and \(\bar x\) is neither a local minimizer nor a local maximizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A QCQP saddle point has both lower- and higher-objective feasible points in every neighborhood.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) is the QCQP feasible set and \(f:F\to\mathbb R\) is its objective.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\forall r>0\;\exists x_r^-,x_r^+\in F\cap B_r(\bar x): f(x_r^-)<f(\bar x)<f(x_r^+).\)

children.title: Negative-Curvature Directions
children.top_down_role: Feasible or critical directions revealing local objective descent through curvature.

knowledge_statements.title: Negative-Curvature Directions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strictly negative Lagrangian curvature along a QCQP critical direction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
At a QCQP KKT triple \(( ar x, ar\lambda, ar
u)\), let \(C( ar x, ar\lambda)\) be the critical cone and set \(H=
abla^2_{xx}L( ar x, ar\lambda, ar
u)\). A vector \(d\) is a negative-curvature direction if \(d\in C( ar x, ar\lambda)\setminus\{0\}\) and \(d^{\mathsf T}Hd<0\). Its existence violates the second-order necessary inequality \(d^{\mathsf T}Hd\ge0\) required at a regular local minimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A negative-curvature direction is a nonzero critical direction on which the Lagrangian Hessian has a negative quadratic form.
assumptions_latex: A constraint qualification supporting the second-order necessary condition holds at \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(d\text{ is negative-curvature}\iff d\in C(\bar x,\bar\lambda)\setminus\{0\}\text{ and }d^{\mathsf T}Hd<0.\)

children.title: Degenerate Saddle Regimes
children.top_down_role: Saddle behavior lacking a directly exposed negative-curvature direction.

knowledge_statements.title: Degenerate Saddle Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Saddles not exposed by strictly negative critical-cone curvature.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\bar x\) be a QCQP saddle point admitting KKT multipliers, with critical cone \(C\) and Lagrangian Hessian \(H\). It lies in a degenerate saddle regime when \(d^{\mathsf T}Hd\ge0\) for every \(d\in C\), while \(d_0^{\mathsf T}Hd_0=0\) for some nonzero \(d_0\in C\). The point has feasible descent and ascent sequences, but no negative-curvature direction in the critical cone; its saddle behavior is therefore not detected by the strict second-order curvature test.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A degenerate saddle has genuine feasible saddle behavior but no strictly negative critical curvature, with some critical direction having zero curvature.
assumptions_latex: \(\bar x\) is a saddle point and satisfies the KKT conditions.
\(C\) and \(H\) are the associated critical cone and Lagrangian Hessian.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\bar x\text{ is degenerate saddle}\iff \bar x\text{ is saddle},\ H\succeq_C0,\ \exists d_0\in C\setminus\{0\}:d_0^{\mathsf T}Hd_0=0.\)

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Combining feasible saddle behavior with critical-cone nonnegativity and a zero-curvature direction is a specialized convention, not a uniquely standard definition of a degenerate saddle. A source is needed to select and support this variant.

knowledge_statements.title: Spurious Local Minima
knowledge_statements.scope_note: QCQP local minima whose values exceed the global optimum.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F\ne\varnothing\) be the feasible set of a QCQP with objective \(f\), and assume the global value \(f^*=\min_{x\in F}f(x)\) is attained. A point \(\bar x\in F\) is a spurious local minimizer if it is a local minimizer of \(f\) over \(F\) and \(f(\bar x)>f^*\). Equivalently, it is locally optimal but does not belong to the global solution set \(S^*=\{x\in F:f(x)=f^*\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A spurious local minimum is locally optimal but has objective value strictly worse than the attained global optimum.
assumptions_latex: \(F\ne\varnothing\) and \(f^*=\min_{x\in F}f(x)\) is finite and attained.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\bar x\text{ is spurious local}\iff \bar x\text{ is local and }f(\bar x)>f^*.\)

children.title: Isolated QCQP Solutions
children.top_down_role: Locally unique feasible stationary or optimal solutions.

knowledge_statements.title: Isolated QCQP Solutions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Isolation within the QCQP global solution set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be the feasible set of a QCQP with objective \(f\), and let \(S^*=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in F}f(x)\) be its nonempty global solution set. A solution \(\bar x\in S^*\) is isolated if there exists \(r>0\) such that \(S^*\cap B_r(\bar x)=\{\bar x\}\). Because \(\bar x\) is globally optimal, this is equivalent to \(\bar x\) being a strict local minimizer of \(f\) over \(F\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A global QCQP solution is isolated when no other global solution lies sufficiently close to it; for a global solution, this is equivalent to strict local minimality.
assumptions_latex: \(F\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is the QCQP feasible set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\bar x\text{ is isolated in }S^*\iff\exists r>0:\ S^*\cap B_r(\bar x)=\{\bar x\}\iff\bar x\text{ is a strict local minimizer over }F.\)

notation.meaning: open Euclidean ball of radius r about the solution

children.title: Nonisolated QCQP Solutions
children.top_down_role: Solution families containing nearby distinct points.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonisolated QCQP Solutions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Accumulation points of the QCQP global solution set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S^*=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in F}f(x)\) be the global solution set of a QCQP. A solution \(\bar x\in S^*\) is nonisolated if every neighborhood of \(\bar x\) contains a distinct point of \(S^*\). Equivalently, for every \(r>0\), the set \((S^*\cap B_r(\bar x))\setminus\{\bar x\}\) is nonempty, or there exists a sequence of distinct solutions \(x_k\in S^*\setminus\{\bar x\}\) satisfying \(x_k\to\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonisolated QCQP solution has distinct global solutions arbitrarily close to it.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\bar x\text{ is nonisolated}\iff\forall r>0,\ (S^*\cap B_r(\bar x))\setminus\{\bar x\}\ne\varnothing.\)

children.title: Positive-Dimensional Solution Sets

knowledge_statements.title: Positive-Dimensional Solution Sets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Semialgebraic local dimension of a QCQP solution set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a QCQP, the global solution set \(S^*=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in F}f(x)\) is semialgebraic whenever the optimum is attained. It is positive-dimensional at \(\bar x\in S^*\) if its local semialgebraic dimension satisfies \(\dim_{\bar x}S^*\ge1\). The solution set is positive-dimensional if this holds at some solution. In particular, such a point is nonisolated, although a nonisolated semialgebraic solution set may have different local dimensions at different points.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A QCQP solution set is positive-dimensional when its local semialgebraic dimension is at least one at some solution.
assumptions_latex: The QCQP has finitely many polynomial equalities and inequalities.
The global optimum is finite and attained.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S^*\text{ is positive-dimensional}\iff\exists\bar x\in S^*:\dim_{\bar x}S^*\ge1.\)

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(x_0\), multiplier estimates, tolerances, and a globalization rule, iteration \(k\) computes \(d_k\) from the quadratic program \[\min_d\ \nabla f(x_k)^\top d+\tfrac12 d^\top B_kd\quad\text{subject to}\quad g_i(x_k)+\nabla g_i(x_k)^\top d\le 0.\] Equalities, when present, are linearized as equalities. A line search or trust region selects an accepted step \(x_{k+1}=x_k+\alpha_kd_k\); multipliers and \(B_k\) are then updated. Terminate when feasibility, stationarity, complementarity, and step tests meet their tolerances; otherwise continue.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize \(x_0\), \(\lambda^0\ge0\), and \(\rho_0>0\). At iteration \(k\), approximately minimize \[\mathcal L_{\rho_k}(x,\lambda^k)=f(x)+\frac{\rho_k}{2}\sum_i\left([g_i(x)+\lambda_i^k/\rho_k]_+^2-(\lambda_i^k/\rho_k)^2\right).\] Set \(x_{k+1}\) to the computed local minimizer and update \(\lambda_i^{k+1}=[\lambda_i^k+\rho_kg_i(x_{k+1})]_+\). Increase \(\rho_k\) when constraint reduction is inadequate. Stop when prescribed feasibility, stationarity, and complementarity residuals are small.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The augmented-Lagrangian interface alternates approximate unconstrained minimization, projected multiplier updates, and adaptive penalty increases until approximate KKT residuals are small.

A feasible point \(x_*\) is a global minimizer if and only if there exists \(\lambda_*\geq0\) such that \[(H+\lambda_*I)x_*=-g,\qquad H+\lambda_*I\succeq0,\qquad \lambda_*(\|x_*\|_2-\Delta)=0.\] If \(H+\lambda_*I\succ0\), the global minimizer is unique. Conversely, every pair satisfying these conditions yields a global minimizer, even when \(H\) is indefinite.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The shifted Hessian is positive definite, and the secular equation identifies the unique boundary minimizer.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In the regular regime, \(H+\lambda_*I\succ0\), so stationarity uniquely gives \(x_*=x(\lambda_*)=-(H+\lambda_*I)^{-1}g\). When \(\lambda_*>0\), complementary slackness reduces the optimality system to the secular equation \[\|x(\lambda_*)\|_2=\Delta.\] On \((\max\{0,-\lambda_{\min}(H)\},\infty)\), the function \(\lambda\mapsto\|x(\lambda)\|_2\) is nonincreasing and is strictly decreasing unless the relevant spectral components of \(g\) vanish. Any root in this interval produces the unique global minimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In the regular regime the shifted Hessian is positive definite, so solving a scalar norm equation yields the unique trust-region minimizer.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The hard case occurs when \(H+\lambda_*I\succeq0\) is singular and \(g\perp E\), where \(E=\ker(H+\lambda_*I)\). Then \(y=-(H+\lambda_*I)^\dagger g\) solves the shifted stationarity equation and is orthogonal to \(E\). Every vector \(z\in E\) satisfying \[\|y+z\|_2=\Delta\] gives a global minimizer \(x_*=y+z\). Such a vector exists when \(\|y\|_2\leq\Delta\); if \(\|y\|_2<\Delta\), the eigenspace component is nonzero and minimizers need not be unique.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In the hard case the shifted Hessian is singular, and a leftmost-eigenvector component completes a pseudoinverse solution to the trust-region boundary.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(B=B^T\) have smallest eigenvalue \(\lambda_1<0\), let the columns of \(Q_1\) span the \(\lambda_1\)-eigenspace, and define
\[
p(\lambda)=-(B+\lambda I)^{-1}g,\qquad \lambda>-\lambda_1.
\]
The ordinary approach remains applicable when the smallest eigenvalue is multiple provided \(Q_1^Tg\ne0\). If \(Q_1^Tg=0\), the equation \(\|p(\lambda)\|=\Delta\) may have no solution in \((-\lambda_1,\infty)\), so open-interval root finding is not generally reliable. If no such root exists, the trust-region optimality multiplier identified by the cited optimality result must satisfy \(\lambda_*=-\lambda_1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A multiple smallest eigenvalue does not itself prevent the usual secular approach when the gradient has a component in its eigenspace. Orthogonality to that eigenspace can eliminate every open-interval radius root; when that happens, the optimal shift is the boundary value minus the smallest eigenvalue.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the strictly convex quadratic, the unique trust-region solution satisfies \[x_\Delta=x_u,\quad \lambda_\Delta=0\quad\text{when}\quad \Delta\geq\|x_u\|_2.\] It is strictly interior when \(\Delta>\|x_u\|_2\), and it lies on the sphere with zero multiplier at \(\Delta=\|x_u\|_2\). When \(0<\Delta<\|x_u\|_2\), the solution satisfies \(\|x_\Delta\|_2=\Delta\), \(\lambda_\Delta>0\), and \((H+\lambda_\Delta I)x_\Delta=-g\). Thus \(\|x_u\|_2\) is the exact interior-boundary threshold.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The linear least-squares trust-region model is \[\min_{\|p\|_2\leq\Delta}\ \frac12\|Ap+r\|_2^2.\] Expanding the squared norm gives \[\frac12\|Ap+r\|_2^2=\frac12p^{\mathsf T}A^{\mathsf T}Ap+(A^{\mathsf T}r)^{\mathsf T}p+\frac12\|r\|_2^2.\] Hence it is the classical trust-region subproblem with \(H=A^{\mathsf T}A\succeq0\) and \(g=A^{\mathsf T}r\); the constant term does not affect minimizers. Rank deficiency of \(A\) corresponds to a singular positive-semidefinite Hessian.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Restricting affine least squares to a ball produces a classical trust-region quadratic whose Hessian is the Gram matrix and whose gradient is the normal-equation residual.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the nonlinear least-squares objective \(\phi(x)=\tfrac12\|F(x)\|_2^2\), replace the residual at \(x+p\) by \(F(x)+J(x)p\). Given \(H\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\) symmetric, \(g\in\mathbb R^n\), \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\), \(b\in\mathbb R^m\), and \(\Delta>0\), the trust-region subproblem with linear constraints is

The inequalities are componentwise; equality constraints may be represented by paired inequalities. The problem is generally nonconvex when \(H\not\succeq0\), although its feasible region is convex.

knowledge_statements.title: Two-Trust-Region Subproblem
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quadratic optimization over the intersection of two ellipsoidal trust regions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(H=H^\top\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\), \(g,c_1,c_2\in\mathbb R^n\), \(M_1,M_2\succeq0\), and \(\Delta_1,\Delta_2>0\). A two-trust-region subproblem is
\[\min_{s\in\mathbb R^n}\ g^\top s+\tfrac12s^\top Hs\quad\text{subject to}\quad (s-c_i)^\top M_i(s-c_i)\leq\Delta_i^2,\quad i=1,2.\]
Euclidean balls arise when \(M_i=I\); positive definite \(M_i\) produce ellipsoids. Indefiniteness of \(H\) makes the objective nonconvex even though both constraints are convex.

knowledge_statements.title: Celis-Dennis-Tapia Subproblem
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Trust-region model with a second norm constraint on a linearized residual.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:

children.title: Moré–Sorensen Framework
children.top_down_role: Structured trust-region solution approaches associated with the Moré–Sorensen framework.

knowledge_statements.title: Moré–Sorensen Framework
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Multiplier-based solution framework for the Euclidean trust-region subproblem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(q(s)=g^\top s+\tfrac12s^\top Hs\) with \(H=H^\top\) and \(\Delta>0\), seek \((s,\lambda)\) satisfying
\[(H+\lambda I)s=-g,\qquad H+\lambda I\succeq0,\qquad \lambda\geq0,\qquad \lambda(\|s\|_2-\Delta)=0.\]
If the unconstrained minimizer exists with norm at most \(\Delta\), output it with \(\lambda=0\). Otherwise update \(\lambda>\max\{0,-\lambda_{\min}(H)\}\), factor \(H+\lambda I\), solve for \(s(\lambda)\), and drive \(\|s(\lambda)\|_2=\Delta\). Stop when the stationarity and radius residuals satisfy prescribed tolerances; treat a singular limiting matrix by a hard-case correction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Solve the trust-region optimality system by iterating on a nonnegative multiplier and repeatedly solving shifted linear systems.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The output \((s,\lambda)\) satisfies the global trust-region optimality conditions to the chosen tolerances.

children.title: Secular-Equation Solvers
children.top_down_role: Trust-region methods organized around scalar secular equations.

knowledge_statements.title: Secular-Equation Solvers
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scalar root-finding for the active-boundary trust-region multiplier.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Assume \(\lambda>\max\{0,-\lambda_{\min}(H)\}\) and define
\[s(\lambda)=-(H+\lambda I)^{-1}g,\qquad \phi(\lambda)=\frac{1}{\|s(\lambda)\|_2}-\frac{1}{\Delta}.\]
Starting from a safeguarded \(\lambda_0\) in this interval, compute \(s_k=s(\lambda_k)\), solve \((H+\lambda_k I)w_k=s_k\), and apply the Newton update
\[\lambda_{k+1}=\lambda_k-\frac{\phi(\lambda_k)}{\phi'(\lambda_k)},\qquad \phi'(\lambda_k)=\frac{s_k^\top w_k}{\|s_k\|_2^3},\]
projecting or bracketing the update when necessary. Stop when \(|\|s_k\|_2-\Delta|\) meets the radius tolerance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Find the active trust-region multiplier by safeguarded Newton or bracketed iteration on the scalar secular equation.
assumptions_latex: The solution is an ordinary active-boundary case.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: At convergence, \((H+\lambda I)s=-g\) and \(\|s\|_2=\Delta\).

children.title: Hard-Case Numerical Boundary
children.top_down_role: Numerically delicate regimes associated with singularity or hard-case behavior.

knowledge_statements.title: Hard-Case Numerical Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Singular multiplier boundary where the ordinary secular equation loses uniqueness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\alpha=\lambda_{\min}(H)<0\), let \(E=\ker(H-\alpha I)\), and suppose \(g\perp E\). At the boundary multiplier \(\lambda_*=-\alpha\), the matrix \(H+\lambda_*I\) is singular. If
\[s_p=-(H+\lambda_*I)^\dagger g,\qquad \|s_p\|_2\leq\Delta,\]
then ordinary inversion-based secular iteration cannot recover every solution. A global solution has the form
\[s_*=s_p+z,\qquad z\in E,\qquad \|s_p+z\|_2=\Delta.\]
Near this boundary, shifted systems become ill-conditioned and the secular derivative may be numerically unreliable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The hard case occurs when the optimal shift makes the Hessian singular and the gradient misses its leftmost eigenspace.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A nullspace correction \(z\) is required whenever \(\|s_p\|_2<\Delta\).

children.title: Standard Eigenvalue Formulations

knowledge_statements.title: Standard Eigenvalue Formulations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quadratic eigenvalue representation of the active-boundary secular equation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For the Euclidean trust-region problem, assume \(H+\lambda I\) is nonsingular and the boundary is active. The conditions
\[(H+\lambda I)s=-g,\qquad \|s\|_2=\Delta\]
are equivalent to
\[\det Q(\lambda)=0,\qquad Q(\lambda):=(H+\lambda I)^2-\Delta^{-2}gg^\top.\]
Thus candidate multipliers are eigenvalues of the quadratic matrix polynomial \(Q\). Equivalently, they are ordinary eigenvalues of the companion matrix
\[\mathcal C=\begin{pmatrix}0&I\\-H^2+\Delta^{-2}gg^\top&-2H\end{pmatrix}.\]
Only roots satisfying the trust-region positivity and stationarity conditions represent global solutions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Encode the active-boundary secular equation as a quadratic eigenvalue problem or its standard companion-matrix linearization.
assumptions_latex: \(H+\lambda I\) is nonsingular at the represented root.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\det Q(\lambda)=0\) provides spectral candidates for the trust-region multiplier.

children.title: Generalized Eigenvalue Pencils

knowledge_statements.title: Generalized Eigenvalue Pencils
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generalized spectral representation for an ellipsoidal trust region.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Consider \(\min_s g^\top s+\tfrac12s^\top Hs\) subject to \(s^\top Bs\leq\Delta^2\), where \(H=H^\top\) and \(B\succ0\). For a nonsingular active-boundary shift, define
\[Q_B(\lambda):=(H+\lambda B)B^{-1}(H+\lambda B)-\Delta^{-2}gg^\top.\]
Then \(\det Q_B(\lambda)=0\). Writing \(Q_B(\lambda)=K_0+\lambda K_1+\lambda^2K_2\), the roots are generalized eigenvalues of
\[\mathcal A-\lambda\mathcal B:=\begin{pmatrix}0&I\\-K_0&-K_1\end{pmatrix}-\lambda\begin{pmatrix}I&0\\0&K_2\end{pmatrix}.\]
Admissible roots must additionally satisfy \(H+\lambda B\succeq0\) and \(\lambda\geq0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Represent an ellipsoidal trust-region secular equation by a generalized companion pencil, then filter its eigenvalues using optimality conditions.
assumptions_latex: \(H+\lambda B\) is nonsingular at the represented root.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\det(\mathcal A-\lambda\mathcal B)=0\) yields the spectral candidates satisfying \(\det Q_B(\lambda)=0\).

knowledge_statements.title: Spectral Root Selection
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Optimality filter selecting the trust-region multiplier from spectral candidates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\Lambda\) be the real roots returned by a spectral formulation of the Euclidean trust-region problem. A root \(\lambda\in\Lambda\) is globally admissible precisely when
\[\lambda\geq0,\qquad H+\lambda I\succeq0,\qquad (H+\lambda I)s=-g,\qquad \|s\|_2\leq\Delta,\qquad \lambda(\|s\|_2-\Delta)=0\]
for some \(s\). In the ordinary active-boundary case, \(H+\lambda I\succ0\), \(s=-(H+\lambda I)^{-1}g\), and the selected root satisfies \(\|s\|_2=\Delta\). Singular roots require the hard-case nullspace correction rather than direct inversion.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Select only real nonnegative spectral roots whose shifted Hessian and associated step satisfy all global trust-region optimality conditions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Any selected pair \((s,\lambda)\) satisfying the displayed system yields a global trust-region minimizer \(s\).

children.title: Steihaug–Toint Truncation
children.top_down_role: Truncated iterative trust-region methods in the Steihaug–Toint family.

knowledge_statements.title: Steihaug–Toint Truncation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conjugate-gradient trust-region iteration truncated at curvature or boundary events.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Initialize \(s_0=0\), \(r_0=g\), and \(p_0=-r_0\). At iteration \(k\), if \(p_k^\top Hp_k\leq0\), choose \(\tau\geq0\) with \(\|s_k+\tau p_k\|_2=\Delta\) and return that boundary point. Otherwise set
\[\alpha_k=\frac{r_k^\top r_k}{p_k^\top Hp_k}.\]
If \(\|s_k+\alpha_kp_k\|_2\geq\Delta\), truncate along \(p_k\) at the boundary and return. Else update \(s_{k+1}=s_k+\alpha_kp_k\), \(r_{k+1}=r_k+\alpha_kHp_k\), and \(p_{k+1}=-r_{k+1}+\beta_kp_k\), where \(\beta_k=r_{k+1}^\top r_{k+1}/(r_k^\top r_k)\). Stop when the residual tolerance is met.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Run conjugate gradients from zero, stopping at convergence, the trust boundary, or the first nonpositive-curvature direction.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The returned step satisfies \(\|s\|_2\leq\Delta\) and lies in the generated Krylov subspace.

children.title: Krylov Subspace Solvers

knowledge_statements.title: Krylov Subspace Solvers
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Matrix-free restriction of a trust-region quadratic to nested Krylov spaces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(q(s)=g^\top s+\tfrac12s^\top Hs\), generate
\[\mathcal K_k(H,g)=\operatorname{span}\{g,Hg,\ldots,H^{k-1}g\}\]
using matrix-vector products with \(H\). Let \(V_k\) have orthonormal columns spanning \(\mathcal K_k(H,g)\), form \(T_k=V_k^\top HV_k\) and \(h_k=V_k^\top g\), and solve
\[\min_{\|y\|_2\leq\Delta}\ h_k^\top y+\tfrac12y^\top T_ky.\]
Set \(s_k=V_ky_k\). Expand the Krylov space until a residual, model-decrease, boundary, negative-curvature, or iteration-limit test is met, and return the latest feasible \(s_k\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Solve progressively larger projected trust-region problems in Krylov subspaces using only Hessian-vector products.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(s_k\in\mathcal K_k(H,g)\), \(\|s_k\|_2\leq\Delta\), and \(s_k\) minimizes the quadratic over that restricted ball.

children.title: Negative-Curvature Termination
children.top_down_role: Method behavior when a Krylov process encounters negative curvature.

knowledge_statements.title: Negative-Curvature Termination
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Truncation rule triggered by a nonpositive-curvature descent direction in a Krylov trust-region method.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(q(s)=g^\top s+\tfrac12s^\top Hs\), where \(H=H^\top\). At an iterate \(s_k\) satisfying \(\|s_k\|_2<\Delta\), let \(p_k\neq0\) satisfy \(p_k^\top Hp_k\leq0\) and \(\nabla q(s_k)^\top p_k<0\). Negative-curvature termination selects the unique positive root \(\tau_+>0\) of
\[\|s_k+\tau p_k\|_2^2=\Delta^2\]
and returns \(s_k+\tau_+p_k\). Along \(\tau\geq0\), the function \(q(s_k+\tau p_k)\) is affine or concave and initially decreasing, so its minimum over the feasible forward segment occurs at the trust-region boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When the current Krylov direction is both a descent direction and a direction of nonpositive curvature, terminate by following it to the forward trust-region boundary.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The returned point \(s_k+\tau_+p_k\) satisfies \(\|s_k+\tau_+p_k\|_2=\Delta\) and minimizes \(q\) over the feasible forward segment \(\{s_k+\tau p_k:\tau\geq0,\ \|s_k+\tau p_k\|_2\leq\Delta\}\).

knowledge_statements.title: Trust-Boundary Termination

knowledge_statements.title: Projection-Based Solvers

knowledge_statements.title: Structured-Norm Geometry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Geometry of a trust region induced by a norm or positive-definite quadratic form.

Its dual norm is \(\|y\|_{W^{-1}}=\sqrt{y^{\mathsf T}W^{-1}y}\).

knowledge_statements.title: Metric Projection Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Existence and uniqueness regimes for variable-metric projection.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a nonempty set \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) and \(M=M^{\mathsf T}\succ0\), define \(P_C^M(y)=\operatorname*{argmin}_{z\in C}\tfrac12\|z-y\|_M^2\). If \(C\) is closed, the projection set is nonempty. If \(C\) is also convex, it is a singleton and \(p=P_C^M(y)\) is characterized by \[\langle M(y-p),z-p\rangle\leq0\quad\text{for every }z\in C.\] Without convexity, existence remains valid for closed \(C\), but uniqueness is not guaranteed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In a positive-definite metric, projections onto nonempty closed sets exist. Convexity guarantees uniqueness and the variational-inequality characterization, while a nonconvex set may have multiple nearest points.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: C\text{ convex}\Longrightarrow P_C^M(y)\text{ is a singleton}

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(A=A^{\mathsf T}\in\mathbb R^{n	imes n}\). The Rayleigh quotient \(R_A(x)=x^{\mathsf T}Ax/(x^{\mathsf T}x)\), defined for \(x
e0\), satisfies \[\min_{x
e0}R_A(x)=\min_{\|x\|_2=1}x^{\mathsf T}Ax=\lambda_{\min}(A),\qquad \max_{x
e0}R_A(x)=\lambda_{\max}(A).\] A unit vector attains either optimum exactly when it lies in the eigenspace associated with the corresponding extreme eigenvalue.

knowledge_statements.title: Generalized-Eigenvalue QCQP
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definite generalized Rayleigh-quotient formulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A=A^{\mathsf T}\) and \(B=B^{\mathsf T}\succ0\). Then \[\min_{x\ne0}\frac{x^{\mathsf T}Ax}{x^{\mathsf T}Bx}=\min_{x^{\mathsf T}Bx=1}x^{\mathsf T}Ax=\lambda_{\min}(A,B),\] where \(\lambda_{\min}(A,B)\) is the smallest \(\lambda\) satisfying \(Av=\lambda Bv\) for some \(v\ne0\). The maximum analog equals \(\lambda_{\max}(A,B)\), and optimizers are normalized generalized eigenvectors for the corresponding extreme eigenvalue.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A quadratic objective on a positive-definite quadratic sphere is solved by the extreme generalized eigenvalues and their eigenvectors.

knowledge_statements.title: Orthogonally Constrained Quadratic Programs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Ky Fan form of a quadratic program on the Stiefel manifold.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A=A^{\mathsf T}\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\) have ordered eigenvalues \(\lambda_1\leq\cdots\leq\lambda_n\), and let \(1\leq r\leq n\). Then \[\min_{X\in\mathbb R^{n\times r},\ X^{\mathsf T}X=I_r}\operatorname{tr}(X^{\mathsf T}AX)=\sum_{i=1}^r\lambda_i.\] The minimum is attained when the columns of \(X\) form an orthonormal basis for an invariant subspace associated with the \(r\) smallest eigenvalues. knowledge_statements.title: Simultaneous-Diagonalization Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Reduction of commuting symmetric QCQP data to diagonal quadratic forms.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A_0,\ldots,A_m\) be real symmetric matrices that commute pairwise. There exists an orthogonal matrix \(U\) such that \(U^{\mathsf T}A_iU=D_i\) is diagonal for every \(i\). Under \(x=Uy\), each quadratic form becomes \[x^{\mathsf T}A_ix=y^{\mathsf T}D_iy=\sum_{j=1}^n(D_i)_{jj}y_j^2.\] Thus a homogeneous QCQP built from these forms depends only on the nonnegative variables \(z_j=y_j^2\), converting its quadratic objective and constraints into linear functions of \(z\).

knowledge_statements.title: Few-Nonconvex-Quadratics Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convex lifting when only one quadratic form remains indefinite.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider a homogeneous QCQP whose quadratic forms are \(x^{\mathsf T}A_ix\). Suppose an invertible change of variables simultaneously diagonalizes the forms and, after introducing \(z_j=y_j^2\), every objective and constraint becomes affine in \(z\). Then the QCQP is equivalent in optimal value to a linear optimization problem over \(z\geq0\) with the transformed affine constraints; any feasible \(z\) lifts to \(y_j=\sigma_j\sqrt{z_j}\), where \(\sigma_j\in\{-1,1\}\). knowledge_statements.title: Symmetry-Induced Hidden Convexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Orbit invariance permits optimization over symmetry-invariant representatives.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a compact group \(G\) act orthogonally on \(\mathbb R^n\), and let \(f\) and the feasible set \(C\) be \(G\)-invariant. Then \(f(gx)=f(x)\) and \(gx\in C\) for all \(g\in G\), so the problem descends exactly to the orbit space: \[\inf_{x\in C}f(x)=\inf_{[x]\in C/G}\bar f([x]),\qquad \bar f([x])=f(x).\] Hidden convexity occurs when invariant coordinates map \(C/G\) to a convex set and express \(\bar f\) as a convex function there.

children.title: Compatible Sign Partitions
children.top_down_role: Variable partitions whose sign patterns support convexifying transformations.

knowledge_statements.title: Compatible Sign Partitions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Signed-graph compatibility condition underlying sign-induced variable transformations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G=(V,E)\) be an undirected interaction graph and let \(\sigma_{ij}\in\{-1,1\}\) prescribe the required relative sign on each edge \(\{i,j\}\in E\). A sign partition is compatible when there exists \(s\in\{-1,1\}^{V}\) such that
\[s_i s_j=\sigma_{ij}\qquad\text{for every }\{i,j\}\in E.\]
Equivalently, every cycle \(C\) of \(G\) satisfies \(\prod_{\{i,j\}\in C}\sigma_{ij}=1\). When such \(s\) exists, the substitution \(x_i=s_i z_i\) simultaneously realizes all prescribed pairwise signs.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A compatible partition assigns signs to vertices so every edge realizes its prescribed relative sign; equivalently, every cycle has positive sign product.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\exists s\in\{-1,1\}^{V}:s_i s_j=\sigma_{ij}\ \forall\{i,j\}\in E\iff \prod_{e\in C}\sigma_e=1\ \forall C.\)
review_flags: Exact signed-bipartite hidden-convexity convention is not identified by the supplied sources.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The signed-graph condition is mathematically standard and the condition role fits the leaf, but no citation connects this sign convention to the intended signed-bipartite hidden-convexity regime.

children.title: Frustrated-Cycle Boundary
children.top_down_role: Interaction cycles whose sign structure obstructs the targeted hidden convexity.

knowledge_statements.title: Frustrated-Cycle Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cycle obstruction to a globally compatible sign transformation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a signed interaction graph \((G,\sigma)\), a cycle \(C\) is frustrated if
\[\prod_{\{i,j\}\in C}\sigma_{ij}=-1.\]
The presence of one frustrated cycle makes the edge equations \(s_i s_j=\sigma_{ij}\) inconsistent: multiplying them around \(C\) gives \(1=-1\). Hence no diagonal sign transformation \(x_i=s_i z_i\) can realize all prescribed edge signs simultaneously. Conversely, if no cycle is frustrated, a compatible signing exists on every connected component.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A negative-sign-product cycle is precisely the obstruction to satisfying all prescribed edge signs by one vertex-sign assignment.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\exists C:\prod_{e\in C}\sigma_e=-1\Rightarrow \nexists s\in\{-1,1\}^{V}:s_i s_j=\sigma_{ij}\ \forall\{i,j\}\in E.\)
review_flags: A source connecting signed-cycle balance specifically to the intended hidden-convexity regime is required.

knowledge_statements.title: Homogenized QCQP Representations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact homogeneous representation of an inhomogeneous real QCQP.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(q_i(x)=x^{\mathsf T}A_i x+2b_i^{\mathsf T}x+c_i\), define
\[Q_i=\begin{pmatrix}c_i&b_i^{\mathsf T}\\ b_i&A_i\end{pmatrix},\qquad y=\begin{pmatrix}1\\x\end{pmatrix}.\]
Then \(q_i(x)=y^{\mathsf T}Q_i y\). Consequently, the QCQP \(\inf\{q_0(x):q_i(x)\le0,\ i=1,\ldots,m\}\) equals
\[\inf\{y^{\mathsf T}Q_0y:y^{\mathsf T}Q_i y\le0,\ i=1,\ldots,m,\ y_0=1\}.\]
The normalization \(y_0=1\) preserves the original affine chart and makes the correspondence with \(x\) bijective.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Appending a constant coordinate converts every affine quadratic into a homogeneous quadratic while preserving the QCQP through the normalization y₀=1.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(q_i(x)=y^{\mathsf T}Q_i y\) under \(y=(1,x)\), and the two displayed optimization problems have equal values.

knowledge_statements.title: Rank-One Matrix Lifting
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact matrix lifting before rank relaxation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(y=(1,x)\) and introduce \(Y=yy^{\mathsf T}\). For every homogenized coefficient matrix \(Q_i\),
\[y^{\mathsf T}Q_i y=\langle Q_i,Y\rangle.\]
Moreover,
\[Y=yy^{\mathsf T}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad Y\succeq0,\ \operatorname{rank}(Y)=1,\ Y_{00}=1,\ Y_{0,1:n}=x^{\mathsf T}.\]
Thus a QCQP is represented exactly by linear functions of \(Y\), the normalization \(Y_{00}=1\), positive semidefiniteness, and the nonconvex rank-one constraint. Dropping only the rank constraint produces the standard Shor lifting.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Quadratic terms become linear matrix inner products after setting Y=yyᵀ; exactness is enforced by positive semidefiniteness, normalization, and rank one.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(y^{\mathsf T}Q_i y=\langle Q_i,Y\rangle\) with exact lifted matrices characterized by \(Y\succeq0\), \(Y_{00}=1\), and \(\operatorname{rank}(Y)=1\).

knowledge_statements.title: Degree-Two Moment-Matrix Viewpoint
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Shor lifting interpreted as a normalized degree-two pseudo-moment matrix.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(L\) be a linear functional on real polynomials of degree at most two with \(L(1)=1\). Writing \(x_i=L(X_i)\) and \(X_{ij}=L(X_iX_j)\), its order-one moment matrix is
\[M_1(L)=L\!\left(\begin{pmatrix}1\\X\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}1\\X\end{pmatrix}^{\!\mathsf T}\right)=\begin{pmatrix}1&x^{\mathsf T}\\x&X\end{pmatrix}.\]
The condition \(L(p^2)\ge0\) for every affine polynomial \(p\) is equivalent to \(M_1(L)\succeq0\). Each quadratic constraint becomes the linear moment inequality \(L(q_i)=\langle Q_i,M_1(L)\rangle\le0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Shor matrix is the degree-two pseudo-moment matrix; its positive semidefiniteness exactly means nonnegativity on squares of affine polynomials.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(L(p^2)\ge0\) for every affine \(p\) if and only if \(M_1(L)\succeq0\), while \(L(q_i)=\langle Q_i,M_1(L)\rangle\).

knowledge_statements.title: Projected-Epigraph Viewpoint
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Original and relaxed epigraphs as projections of lifted feasible sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a minimization QCQP, define the exact lifted epigraph
\[\mathcal E_1=\{(t,x,Y):Y=(1,x)(1,x)^{\mathsf T},\ \langle Q_0,Y\rangle\le t,\ \langle Q_i,Y\rangle\le0\ \forall i\}.\]
Its projection onto \((t,x)\) is exactly the QCQP epigraph. Replacing \(Y=(1,x)(1,x)^{\mathsf T}\) by
\[\begin{pmatrix}1&x^{\mathsf T}\\x&X\end{pmatrix}\succeq0\]
defines a convex lifted set whose \((t,x)\)-projection contains the original epigraph. Minimizing \(t\) over that projection yields the projected Shor lower bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The QCQP epigraph is a projection of a rank-one lifted set; dropping rank gives a convex projected outer approximation and a lower bound.
assumptions_latex: All QCQP constraints have the form \(q_i(x)\le0\).
The problem is a minimization problem.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{proj}_{t,x}(\mathcal E_1)=\operatorname{epi}_{\mathrm{feas}}(q_0)\), and the rank-relaxed projection contains this epigraph.

knowledge_statements.title: Primal Shor Relaxation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dense primal semidefinite relaxation of an inequality-form QCQP.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For the QCQP
\[p^*=\inf\{q_0(x):q_i(x)\le0,\ i=1,\ldots,m\},\]
with homogenized matrices \(Q_i\), the primal Shor relaxation is
\[p_{\mathrm S}=\inf_{Y\in\mathbb S^{n+1}}\{\langle Q_0,Y\rangle:\langle Q_i,Y\rangle\le0,\ i=1,\ldots,m,\ Y_{00}=1,\ Y\succeq0\}.\]
Every feasible \(x\) supplies the feasible rank-one matrix \(Y=(1,x)(1,x)^{\mathsf T}\). Therefore \(p_{\mathrm S}\le p^*\) under the extended-real convention, so the relaxation gives a lower bound for minimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dropping rank one from the lifted QCQP gives an SDP; every original feasible point lifts feasibly, so its optimum is a lower bound.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(p_{\mathrm S}\le p^*\).

knowledge_statements.title: Shor Semidefinite Bound
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Lower-bound property of the primal Shor SDP.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(p_{\mathrm S}\) be the value of the primal Shor relaxation and \(p^*\) the value of the original minimization QCQP. Since the rank-one lift of every QCQP-feasible point is Shor-feasible with the same objective value,
\[p_{\mathrm S}\le p^*.\]
If an optimal Shor matrix \(Y^*\) has rank one, then \(Y^*=y^*{y^*}^{\mathsf T}\) with \(y_0^*=1\) after a harmless sign choice, and \(x^*=y^*_{1:n}\) is QCQP-feasible with objective \(p_{\mathrm S}\). Thus rank-one attainment certifies exactness.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Shor value is a minimization lower bound, and an attained rank-one Shor solution recovers a globally optimal QCQP point.
assumptions_latex: The QCQP and its Shor relaxation use the same homogenized matrices.
An optimal Shor matrix exists for the rank-one exactness assertion.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(p_{\mathrm S}\le p^*\), and \(\operatorname{rank}(Y^*)=1\Rightarrow p_{\mathrm S}=p^*\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(q_i(x)=x^{\mathsf T}A_i x+2b_i^{\mathsf T}x+c_i\), define
\[g(\lambda)=\inf_{x\in\mathbb R^n}\left(q_0(x)+\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_iq_i(x)\right),\qquad \lambda\ge0.\]
The Lagrangian dual bound is \(d_{\mathrm L}=\sup_{\lambda\ge0}g(\lambda)\). Weak duality gives \(d_{\mathrm L}\le p^*\). Moreover, using the shard's homogeneous coordinate order \((1,x)\), \(g(\lambda)\ge\gamma\) is equivalent to
\[\begin{pmatrix}c_0+\sum_i\lambda_i c_i-\gamma&(b_0+\sum_i\lambda_i b_i)^{\mathsf T}\\b_0+\sum_i\lambda_i b_i&A_0+\sum_i\lambda_iA_i\end{pmatrix}\succeq0,\]
so computing \(d_{\mathrm L}\) is an SDP.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Maximizing the infimum of the quadratic Lagrangian over nonnegative multipliers gives a QCQP lower bound expressible by one linear matrix inequality.

knowledge_statements.title: Bound-Equivalence Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strong-duality regime equating primal Shor and Lagrangian-dual bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Consider the primal Shor SDP with finite optimal value \(p_{\mathrm S}\), and let \(d_{\mathrm L}\) be the QCQP Lagrangian dual value. The conic dual of the primal Shor formulation is precisely the LMI formulation of \(d_{\mathrm L}\). If the Shor SDP is strictly feasible, meaning that some \(Y\succ0\) satisfies \(Y_{00}=1\) and \(\langle Q_i,Y\rangle<0\) for every inequality constraint, then semidefinite strong duality yields
\[p_{\mathrm S}=d_{\mathrm L},\]
and the dual optimum is attained. The analogous conclusion holds under dual strict feasibility when the primal value is finite.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Shor SDP and quadratic Lagrangian dual have equal values under primal or dual semidefinite Slater conditions, with attainment on the opposite side.
assumptions_latex: The primal Shor SDP is feasible and has finite value.
Either the primal or dual SDP satisfies the corresponding strict-feasibility condition.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(p_{\mathrm S}=d_{\mathrm L}\), with attainment on the side opposite the strictly feasible side.

knowledge_statements.title: Equivalence Failure Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Loss of conic regularity at the Shor–Lagrangian equivalence boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
If neither the primal Shor SDP nor its LMI dual has a strictly feasible point, conic strong duality is no longer guaranteed. Weak duality alone remains:
\[d_{\mathrm L}\le p_{\mathrm S}\le p^*.\]
At this boundary, equality \(d_{\mathrm L}=p_{\mathrm S}\) may still hold for a particular QCQP, but it cannot be inferred solely from primal feasibility and finiteness; a positive duality gap or nonattainment can occur in semidefinite programming. Thus failure of Slater-type regularity is a failure boundary for the general bound-equivalence theorem, not by itself a certificate that a gap exists.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Without primal or dual SDP strict feasibility, only weak duality is assured; equality may persist, but gaps or nonattainment are no longer excluded.
assumptions_latex: The primal Shor SDP and its conic dual are formulated consistently.
Neither side is assumed strictly feasible.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(d_{\mathrm L}\le p_{\mathrm S}\le p^*\); equality and attainment require separate justification.

knowledge_statements.title: Projected Shor Relaxation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Original-variable projection of the dense Shor spectrahedron.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Write the Shor matrix as
\[Y=\begin{pmatrix}1&x^{\mathsf T}\\x&X\end{pmatrix}.\]
The projected Shor feasible region is
\[\mathcal F_{\mathrm{proj}}=\left\{x\in\mathbb R^n:\exists X\in\mathbb S^n,\ Y\succeq0,\ \langle Q_i,Y\rangle\le0\ \text{for }i=1,\ldots,m\right\}.\]
Every QCQP-feasible \(x\) belongs to \(\mathcal F_{\mathrm{proj}}\) by choosing \(X=xx^{\mathsf T}\). Hence \(\mathcal F_{\mathrm{proj}}\) is a convex outer approximation of the original feasible set. Adding \(\langle Q_0,Y\rangle\le t\) gives its projected epigraph form.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Projecting the Shor spectrahedron onto the original variables gives a convex outer approximation containing every QCQP-feasible point.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\{x:q_i(x)\le0\ \forall i\}\subseteq\mathcal F_{\mathrm{proj}}\), and \(\mathcal F_{\mathrm{proj}}\) is convex.
