children.title: Scaling-Sensitive Failure Regimes
children.top_down_role: Numerical regimes where poor magnitude balance degrades solution or certificate reliability.

assumptions_latex: The QCQP data are represented in floating-point arithmetic with unit roundoff \(u\).
A nonsingular diagonal change of variables \(x=Dy\) is permitted.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If the scaled backward error bound is small but its amplification by \(\kappa(D)\) or the data dynamic range is not, then unscaled feasibility or optimality is not reliably certified.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-precision failure caused by translating residuals through an ill-conditioned scaling.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider a QCQP transformed by \(x=Dy\), where \(D\) is nonsingular and diagonal. Suppose a numerical method returns \(\widehat y\) with a scaled residual or backward error of order \(u\). Mapping the result back can amplify perturbations by factors involving \(\|D\|\), \(\|D^{-1}\|\), and the norms of the original quadratic data. Thus a small scaled residual does not imply a small original-coordinate residual when \(\kappa(D)u\) or the original data dynamic range is not small. In this regime, stopping tests and feasibility declarations based only on scaled quantities can fail.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Ill-conditioned scaling can turn a small residual in equilibrated coordinates into a large original-coordinate error, invalidating scale-blind stopping and feasibility tests.
knowledge_statements.title: Scaling-Sensitive Failure Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary role fits, but the dependence of original-coordinate residuals on scaling and data norms is formulation-specific. An authoritative numerical-analysis source is required before the stated amplification regime can be assessed reliably.

children.title: Near-Singular Regimes
children.top_down_role: QCQP data or relaxation systems with nearly singular matrix structure.

assumptions_latex: A symmetric matrix \(Q\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\) represents a quadratic objective, constraint, or KKT block.
A scale \(\tau>0\) and tolerance \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\) are fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The data are in a near-singular regime exactly when \(\sigma_{\min}(Q)\le \varepsilon\tau\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Operational relative definition for spectral degeneracy of a QCQP matrix block.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Q\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\) be symmetric and let \(\tau>0\) be a reference scale, typically \(\tau=\|Q\|_2\). For a prescribed \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\), call \(Q\) near-singular when \[\sigma_{\min}(Q)\leq \varepsilon\tau.\] If \(Q\) is nonsingular and \(\tau=\sigma_{\max}(Q)\), this is equivalent to \(\kappa_2(Q)\geq \varepsilon^{-1}\). For an exactly singular matrix the condition holds for every positive \(\varepsilon\). The tolerance and reference scale are part of the regime specification and must be reported.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A QCQP matrix block is near-singular when its smallest singular value is small relative to a declared spectral scale and tolerance.
knowledge_statements.title: Near-Singular Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: This is a coherent operational condition, but it is a declared threshold convention rather than a universal characterization of near-singularity. The reference scale and convention require a source.

children.title: Spectral-Clustering Regimes
children.top_down_role: QCQP instances with tightly grouped eigenvalues or singular values.

assumptions_latex: A symmetric matrix \(Q\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\) has ordered eigenvalues \(\lambda_1\leq\cdots\leq\lambda_n\).
A partition of the ordered spectrum and within-cluster tolerance \(\delta\geq0\) are specified.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The matrix is spectrally clustered when every cluster has diameter at most \(\delta\), with intercluster gaps recorded separately.

notation.meaning: Ordered eigenvalues of the symmetric matrix

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Operational definition separating within-cluster diameter from between-cluster gaps.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Q\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\) be symmetric with \(\lambda_1\leq\cdots\leq\lambda_n\). Given indices \(0=k_0<k_1<\cdots<k_r=n\), define cluster \(C_j=\{\lambda_{k_{j-1}+1},\ldots,\lambda_{k_j}\}\). The spectrum is \(\delta\)-clustered relative to this partition when \[\max C_j-\min C_j\leq\delta\quad\text{for every }j.\] Its consecutive cluster separations are \(\gamma_j=\lambda_{k_j+1}-\lambda_{k_j}\) for \(j<r\). A clustering regime records both \(\delta\) and the \(\gamma_j\); clustering alone does not require large separation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A spectral-clustering regime groups ordered eigenvalues into blocks of small within-block diameter while recording, but not presupposing, the gaps between blocks.
knowledge_statements.title: Spectral-Clustering Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits the leaf and consistently distinguishes cluster diameter from separation, but no source supports this particular clustering convention.

children.title: Cluster-Separation Sensitivity
children.top_down_role: Reliability changes associated with shrinking spectral separation.

assumptions_latex: A symmetric matrix \(Q\) has two adjacent spectral clusters separated by \(\gamma>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The invariant subspace is sensitive at scale \(\|E\|_2/\gamma\), and stable cluster identification requires perturbations small relative to \(\gamma\).

notation.meaning: Unperturbed separation between the selected cluster and the remaining spectrum
Largest principal angle between invariant subspaces

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Symmetric invariant-subspace sensitivity under a positive spectral gap.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Q\) and \(Q+E\) be real symmetric. Let \(\mathcal U\) be an invariant subspace of \(Q\) associated with a spectral cluster separated from the remaining spectrum by \(\gamma>0\), and let \(\widehat{\mathcal U}\) denote the corresponding perturbed invariant subspace whenever the cluster remains identifiable. A Davis--Kahan-type estimate has the form \[\|\sin\Theta(\mathcal U,\widehat{\mathcal U})\|_2\leq \frac{\|E\|_2}{\gamma_*},\] where \(\gamma_*\) is the applicable separation between the compared spectral sets. Consequently, sensitivity grows inversely with cluster separation, and no small-angle guarantee follows when the perturbation is comparable to the gap.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Invariant subspaces associated with a spectral cluster become increasingly sensitive as the separating eigenvalue gap shrinks relative to the perturbation norm.
knowledge_statements.title: Cluster-Separation Sensitivity

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The sensitivity property fits the container and appropriately leaves the applicable Davis–Kahan separation as gamma-star, but the precise hypotheses and denominator require an authoritative theorem locator.

knowledge_statements.title: Hard-Case Numerics
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical Euclidean trust-region hard case and its singular shifted-system mechanism.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the trust-region subproblem \[\min_{\|s\|_2\leq\Delta}\;g^Ts+\tfrac12s^THs,\] the hard case occurs when \(g\) is orthogonal to an eigenspace associated with \(\lambda_{\min}(H)<0\) and the minimum-norm solution of \((H-\lambda_{\min}(H)I)s=-g\) has norm below \(\Delta\). Then \(\lambda_*=-\lambda_{\min}(H)\), so \(H+\lambda_*I\) is singular, and an optimal step has the form \(s_*=s_0+z\), where \(z\in\ker(H+\lambda_*I)\) is chosen so that \(\|s_*\|_2=\Delta\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The trust-region hard case makes the optimally shifted Hessian singular and requires a minimum-eigenvector component to attain the boundary solution.
assumptions_latex: The trust-region subproblem is \(\min_s g^Ts+\tfrac12s^THs\) subject to \(\|s\|_2\leq\Delta\), with symmetric \(H\).
The smallest eigenvalue of \(H\) is negative.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: In the hard case, the optimal multiplier reaches \(-\lambda_{\min}(H)\), the shifted system is singular, and a nullspace component is needed to reach the boundary.

children.title: Relaxation Size Growth
children.top_down_role: Growth of lifted variables, constraints, blocks, and matrix dimensions.

assumptions_latex: A degree-\(2d\) moment or sum-of-squares relaxation is formed for a polynomial QCQP in \(n\) variables.
The dense monomial basis of degrees at most \(d\) is used.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The principal semidefinite block has order \(\binom{n+d}{d}\), so dense storage grows quadratically in this binomial quantity.

notation.meaning: Number of monomials of degree at most \(d\)

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dense monomial-basis growth for moment or sum-of-squares relaxations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(n\) variables, the vector of all monomials of total degree at most \(d\) has length \[N_d=\binom{n+d}{d}.\] Hence a dense order-\(d\) moment or sum-of-squares relaxation contains a principal symmetric positive-semidefinite matrix of order \(N_d\). Merely storing this block densely requires \(N_d(N_d+1)/2\) scalar entries, and generic dense linear-algebra costs are at least quadratic in \(N_d\) for storage and typically cubic in \(N_d\) per factorization. Additional localizing blocks increase these counts according to their degree-adjusted monomial bases.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dense moment and sum-of-squares relaxations grow with a binomial monomial count, producing quadratic storage and typically cubic factorization growth in block order.
knowledge_statements.title: Relaxation Size Growth

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The complexity-bound role and monomial count are appropriate, but the moment/SOS block construction and dense factorization-cost statement require an authoritative relaxation reference.

children.title: Memory Capacity Limits
children.top_down_role: Storage ceilings affecting relaxation construction, factorization, or solution.

assumptions_latex: A dense symmetric relaxation block of order \(N\) is stored using \(b\) bytes per scalar.
At most \(M\) bytes are available for this block.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Dense storage is possible only if \(bN(N+1)/2\leq M\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Necessary capacity condition for explicitly storing one dense symmetric relaxation block.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A dense symmetric matrix of order \(N\) has \(N(N+1)/2\) independent scalar entries. If each stored scalar occupies \(b\) bytes and the usable memory budget is \(M\) bytes, explicit packed storage of the block is feasible only if \[b\frac{N(N+1)}{2}\leq M.\] Equivalently, \[N\leq \left\lfloor\frac{\sqrt{1+8M/b}-1}{2}\right\rfloor.\] This is only a necessary capacity test for a solver: constraint matrices, factors, work arrays, indexing, and replication require additional memory.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A dense symmetric relaxation block fits only when its packed entries fit the memory budget; solver overhead makes this necessary but not sufficient.
knowledge_statements.title: Memory Capacity Limits

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The packed-storage condition is mathematically consistent and correctly identified as necessary rather than sufficient, but the candidate supplies neither a source nor an explicit standard-field rationale.

children.title: Size-Memory Tradeoffs
children.top_down_role: Representation choices that exchange relaxation detail for reduced storage demand.

knowledge_statements.title: Size-Memory Tradeoffs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dense block-size tradeoff between representation strength, storage, and factorization cost.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a conic relaxation with dense symmetric blocks of orders \(N_1,\ldots,N_r\), explicit block storage is \[\Theta\!\left(\sum_{j=1}^r N_j^2\right),\] while independent dense factorizations require \[\Theta\!\left(\sum_{j=1}^r N_j^3\right)\] arithmetic in the standard dense model. Replacing one block of order \(N\) by smaller blocks can reduce these resources because \(\sum_jN_j^2\) and \(\sum_jN_j^3\) may be much smaller than \(N^2\) and \(N^3\). Such a replacement preserves the original relaxation only when the decomposition is mathematically valid; arbitrary block splitting generally weakens or changes it.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Relaxation strength and block size compete with memory and factorization cost; valid structural decomposition can reduce resources, but arbitrary splitting changes the relaxation.
assumptions_latex: A relaxation is represented by symmetric semidefinite blocks of orders \(N_1,\ldots,N_r\).
Blocks and factorization workspaces are stored explicitly.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Memory scales as \(\Theta(\sum_jN_j^2)\), while dense factorization work scales as \(\Theta(\sum_jN_j^3)\); decomposition reduces memory only by changing block structure.

assumptions_latex: A conic relaxation has primal residual \(r_p\), dual residual \(r_d\), and reported primal-dual gap \(g\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The solution is \(\varepsilon\)-accurate only when all normalized residual and gap tests are at most \(\varepsilon\); otherwise exact feasibility or certification cannot be inferred.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Residual-based operational meaning of a low-accuracy conic relaxation solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given positive normalization scales \(s_p,s_d,s_g\), call a computed primal-dual conic pair \(\varepsilon\)-accurate when \[\frac{\|r_p\|}{s_p}\leq\varepsilon,\qquad \frac{\|r_d\|}{s_d}\leq\varepsilon,\qquad \frac{|g|}{s_g}\leq\varepsilon.\] A low-accuracy solution uses an \(\varepsilon\) too large for the downstream QCQP claim being made. Such a pair may provide an approximate relaxation bound, but it does not by itself establish exact cone membership, exact feasibility, or a rigorous optimality certificate. Any bound transferred to the original QCQP must include residual effects and the relaxation direction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A conic solution is low-accuracy when normalized residuals or gap are too large for the intended QCQP conclusion; exact certification then does not follow.
knowledge_statements.title: Low-Accuracy Conic Solutions

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition fits the low-accuracy leaf, but residual definitions, normalization scales, and the validity of transferred QCQP bounds depend on the conic formulation and solver convention. A specific stopping-criteria source is required.

knowledge_statements.title: Finite-Precision Certificate Reliability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Reliability criterion based on validated residual bounds and strict numerical margins.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a floating-point primal-dual tuple claim tolerance-qualified feasibility, a bound, or optimality for a QCQP or its conic relaxation. Recompute every defining residual in the original coordinates using validated arithmetic, such as interval arithmetic or directed rounding, obtaining enclosures \(r_i\in[\underline r_i,\overline r_i]\). The tuple supports the claimed numerical certificate only when the validated bounds verify every required residual tolerance, every inequality with the required directed margin, and every cone-membership or semidefiniteness condition without an unresolved sign or spectral crossing. Small unvalidated floating-point residuals alone do not establish such a certificate when rounding-error bounds can exceed the available feasibility or spectral margin. A nonzero residual tolerance does not by itself establish exact feasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A tolerance-qualified floating-point certificate is reliable only when validated error bounds preserve every required sign, cone condition, and residual margin in original coordinates; this does not by itself prove exact feasibility.
assumptions_latex: A purported QCQP certificate consists of floating-point primal-dual variables and multipliers.
Residuals are recomputed in the original, unscaled problem data using a validated error-bounding method.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The tolerance-qualified certificate is numerically reliable only if validated bounds verify the required cone membership, sign conditions, and residual inequalities with sufficient margins; exact feasibility requires additional exact justification.

children.title: QCQP Application-Model Interface Taxonomy
children.top_down_role: Canonical model templates and bounded navigation interfaces; detailed domain theory remains in the owning chapters.

assumptions_latex: The residual model is affine: \(r(s)=As-b\), with \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) and \(b\in\mathbb R^m\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The constrained least-squares model is a QCQP with Hessian \(A^TA\), linear term \(-A^Tb\), and constraint \(s^Ts\leq\Delta^2\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Affine least-squares model constrained by a Euclidean trust region.

source_refs.locator: 4.4.1 Least-Squares Problems p. 68
5.3 Linear Least-Squares Problems p. 106

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The least-squares trust-region problem \[\min_{s\in\mathbb R^n}\ \frac12\|As-b\|_2^2\quad\text{subject to}\quad\|s\|_2\leq\Delta\] is equivalently the QCQP \[\min_{s\in\mathbb R^n}\ \frac12s^TA^TAs-(A^Tb)^Ts+\frac12\|b\|_2^2\quad\text{subject to}\quad s^Ts\leq\Delta^2.\] Thus its quadratic Hessian is \(A^TA\succeq0\), its linear coefficient is \(-A^Tb\), and its sole quadratic constraint is a Euclidean ball. The constant term may be omitted without changing minimizers.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Affine least squares over a Euclidean ball is a convex QCQP with Hessian A-transpose-A and one quadratic trust-region constraint.
knowledge_statements.title: Least-Squares Trust-Region Model

source_witnesses.locator: 4.4.1 Least-Squares Problems p. 68
5.3 Linear Least-Squares Problems p. 106

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Introducing \(X=xx^*\) converts each intensity equation to \(a_i^*Xa_i=y_i\), with \(X\succeq0\) and \(\operatorname{rank}(X)=1\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Rank-one semidefinite lifting of quadratic intensity measurements.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For quadratic intensity measurements \(y_i=|a_i^*x|^2\), define the Hermitian matrix \(X=xx^*\). Then \[|a_i^*x|^2=x^*a_ia_i^*x=\operatorname{tr}(a_ia_i^*X)=a_i^*Xa_i.\] Hence exact phase retrieval is represented by the affine equations \(a_i^*Xa_i=y_i\), together with \(X\succeq0\) and \(\operatorname{rank}(X)=1\). Dropping the rank constraint gives a convex semidefinite relaxation; retaining it gives an exact lifted nonconvex formulation. Any recovered factor is identifiable only up to multiplication by a scalar of unit modulus.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Phase retrieval lifts quadratic intensities to linear equations in a positive semidefinite rank-one matrix; dropping rank yields an SDP relaxation.
knowledge_statements.title: Phase-Retrieval QCQP Interface

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The exact rank-one lifting and SDP-relaxation distinction are mathematically standard and fit the representation leaf, but no inspectable source or locator is supplied. The approximate-measurement assumption also requires a source clarifying how noise is modeled beyond the exact equations shown.

knowledge_statements.title: Quadratically Constrained Estimation Interface
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Constrained least-squares estimation with quadratic prior or feasibility information.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given the observation model \(b=Ax+\varepsilon\), a quadratically constrained estimator is represented by
\[
\widehat{x}\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in\mathbb{R}^n}\|Ax-b\|_2^2
\quad\text{subject to}\quad
x^{\mathsf T}Q_i x+2q_i^{\mathsf T}x+r_i\le 0,
\quad i=1,\ldots,m.
\]
The objective and constraints are quadratic functions of the unknown parameter, so this is a QCQP. Quadratic equality information may instead be imposed using equality constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Estimate an unknown real vector by minimizing squared residuals subject to finitely many quadratic prior, structural, or feasibility constraints.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\widehat{x}\) is obtained from a quadratically constrained quadratic optimization problem.

notation.meaning: coefficients of the ith quadratic constraint

children.title: Max-Cut QCQP Formulation
children.top_down_role: Quadratic optimization representation of the Max-Cut problem.

knowledge_statements.title: Max-Cut QCQP Formulation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Binary-sign QCQP representation of weighted undirected Max-Cut.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For an undirected graph \(G=(V,E)\) with nonnegative edge weights \(w_{ij}\), assign a sign \(x_i\in\{-1,1\}\) to each vertex. An edge is cut exactly when \(x_i x_j=-1\). Hence weighted Max-Cut has the QCQP representation
\[
\operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm{MC}}=
\max_{x\in\mathbb{R}^{|V|}}
\frac14\sum_{\{i,j\}\in E}w_{ij}(x_i-x_j)^2
=
\max_{x\in\mathbb{R}^{|V|}}
\frac12\sum_{\{i,j\}\in E}w_{ij}(1-x_i x_j)
\quad\text{subject to}\quad x_i^2=1\ \text{for all }i\in V.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Represent each side of a cut by a sign. Quadratic sign constraints enforce binary assignments, and the quadratic objective equals the total weight crossing the cut.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm{MC}}\) equals the displayed binary QCQP optimum.

notation.meaning: sign identifying the side containing vertex i

children.title: Max-Cut SDP Relaxation Interface
children.top_down_role: Semidefinite lifting and relaxation structure associated with the Max-Cut QCQP.

knowledge_statements.title: Max-Cut SDP Relaxation Interface
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard lifted semidefinite relaxation of the binary-sign Max-Cut QCQP.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Introduce \(X=xx^{\mathsf T}\), so that \(x_i x_j=X_{ij}\), \(X_{ii}=1\), \(X\succeq0\), and \(\operatorname{rank}(X)=1\). Dropping only the rank constraint gives the semidefinite relaxation
\[
\operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm{SDP}}=
\max_{X\in\mathbb{S}^{|V|}}
\frac12\sum_{\{i,j\}\in E}w_{ij}(1-X_{ij})
\quad\text{subject to}\quad
X\succeq0,\qquad X_{ii}=1\ \text{for all }i\in V.
\]
Every feasible sign vector produces a feasible SDP matrix through \(X=xx^{\mathsf T}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Lift sign products into a positive-semidefinite matrix and discard the rank-one condition, obtaining a convex SDP whose feasible set contains every Max-Cut solution.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) and \(w_{ij}\ge0\) define a weighted Max-Cut instance.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm{SDP}}\ge\operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm{MC}}\).

notation.meaning: lifted matrix representing pairwise sign products

children.title: QCQP-to-SDP Gap Interface
children.top_down_role: Navigation boundary between the discrete QCQP value, SDP bound, and rounded solution quality.

knowledge_statements.title: QCQP-to-SDP Gap Interface
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Instance-wise additive and multiplicative gaps between Max-Cut QCQP and SDP values.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a weighted Max-Cut instance with QCQP value \(v_Q=\operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm{MC}}\) and relaxation value \(v_S=\operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm{SDP}}\), define the additive relaxation gap by
\[
g_{\mathrm{add}}=v_S-v_Q\ge0.
\]
When \(v_Q>0\), define the multiplicative gap by
\[
g_{\mathrm{mult}}=\frac{v_S}{v_Q}\ge1.
\]
The relaxation is exact on the instance precisely when \(g_{\mathrm{add}}=0\), equivalently when \(g_{\mathrm{mult}}=1\) whenever the latter is defined.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The SDP gap measures how much the lifted relaxation exceeds the true Max-Cut QCQP value; zero additive gap means exact relaxation.
assumptions_latex: \(v_Q\) and \(v_S\) use the same graph and edge weights.
\(v_Q>0\) when the multiplicative gap is used.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(g_{\mathrm{add}}\ge0\), \(g_{\mathrm{mult}}\ge1\), and exactness is equivalent to equality of the two optimal values.

source_refs.locator: 2.14.3 SDP Programming p. 84

source_witnesses.locator: 2.14.3 SDP Programming p. 84

knowledge_statements.title: Binary Quadratic Optimization Interface
knowledge_statements.scope_note: General unconstrained binary quadratic model expressed as an equality-constrained QCQP.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A binary quadratic optimization problem with symmetric matrix \(Q\in\mathbb{S}^n\), linear coefficient \(c\in\mathbb{R}^n\), and scalar \(d\in\mathbb{R}\) is
\[
\min_{x\in\{0,1\}^n}x^{\mathsf T}Qx+c^{\mathsf T}x+d.
\]
It is equivalently the QCQP
\[
\min_{x\in\mathbb{R}^n}x^{\mathsf T}Qx+c^{\mathsf T}x+d
\quad\text{subject to}\quad
x_i^2-x_i=0,
\quad i=1,\ldots,n.
\]
Over the real numbers, each equation is equivalent to \(x_i\in\{0,1\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Replace every binary restriction by the quadratic equation x squared equals x, producing an equivalent equality-constrained QCQP.
assumptions_latex: The decision variables are real before the binary equations are imposed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:x_i^2-x_i=0\ \forall i\}=\{0,1\}^n\).

source_refs.locator: 3.9 The GOP for Quadratically Constrained Problems p. 96

source_witnesses.locator: 3.9 The GOP for Quadratically Constrained Problems p. 96

knowledge_statements.title: Quadratic Assignment Interface
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Permutation-matrix QCQP representation of the quadratic assignment problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given flow matrix \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}\) and distance matrix \(B\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}\), the quadratic assignment problem is
\[
\min_{P\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}}
\sum_{i,j,k,l=1}^n A_{ij}B_{kl}P_{ik}P_{jl}
\]
subject to
\[
\sum_{k=1}^nP_{ik}=1,\quad
\sum_{i=1}^nP_{ik}=1,\quad
P_{ik}^2-P_{ik}=0
\quad\text{for all }i,k.
\]
The constraints make \(P\) a permutation matrix, so the objective assigns facilities to locations and sums pairwise flow-distance costs.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Use a binary permutation matrix to assign facilities to locations; the quadratic objective couples pairs of assignments through flow and distance coefficients.
assumptions_latex: Each facility and each location participates in exactly one assignment.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The feasible matrices are exactly the \(n\times n\) permutation matrices.

notation.meaning: flow from facility i to facility j
distance from location k to location l
indicator that facility i is assigned to location k

knowledge_statements.title: Beamforming QCQP Interface
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Complex downlink beamforming with minimum-power objective and user SINR constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For channels \(h_k\in\mathbb{C}^{N}\), beamformers \(w_k\in\mathbb{C}^{N}\), noise powers \(\sigma_k^2>0\), and SINR targets \(\gamma_k>0\), minimum-power downlink beamforming is
\[
\min_{w_1,\ldots,w_K}\sum_{k=1}^K\|w_k\|_2^2
\quad\text{subject to}\quad
|h_k^*w_k|^2-\gamma_k\sum_{j\ne k}|h_k^*w_j|^2
\ge\gamma_k\sigma_k^2,
\quad k=1,\ldots,K.
\]
Each squared magnitude is a Hermitian quadratic form, so the model is a complex QCQP.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Choose user beamformers minimizing total transmit power while quadratic SINR inequalities guarantee each user’s desired signal relative to interference and noise.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The minimum-power beamforming model is a complex QCQP in \((w_1,\ldots,w_K)\).

source_refs.locator: 3.9 The GOP for Quadratically Constrained Problems p. 96

source_witnesses.locator: 3.9 The GOP for Quadratically Constrained Problems p. 96

knowledge_statements.title: Constant-Modulus QCQP Interface
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Hermitian quadratic optimization with prescribed component magnitudes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(Q\in\mathbb{H}^n\), \(c\in\mathbb{C}^n\), and prescribed squared moduli \(\rho_i>0\), a constant-modulus QCQP has the form
\[
\min_{z\in\mathbb{C}^n}
z^*Qz+2\operatorname{Re}(c^*z)+d
\quad\text{subject to}\quad
|z_i|^2=\rho_i,
\quad i=1,\ldots,n.
\]
When \(\rho_i=1\) for every \(i\), the feasible set is the complex unit torus. Each modulus equality is a nonconvex quadratic equality in the real and imaginary parts of \(z\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Optimize a Hermitian quadratic function while fixing every component's squared magnitude, yielding a nonconvex QCQP over a product of circles.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The feasible set is \(\{z\in\mathbb{C}^n:|z_i|^2=\rho_i\ \forall i\}\).

notation.meaning: prescribed squared modulus of component i

children.title: Multicast QCQP Interface
children.top_down_role: QCQP model structures arising in multicast transmission design.

knowledge_statements.title: Multicast QCQP Interface
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Single-group physical-layer multicast beamforming with minimum transmit power.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(h_i\in\mathbb{C}^{N}\) be the channel to receiver \(i\), let \(w\in\mathbb{C}^{N}\) be a common beamformer, and let \(\eta_i>0\) be the required received signal power. The multicast design problem is
\[
\min_{w\in\mathbb{C}^{N}}\|w\|_2^2
\quad\text{subject to}\quad
|h_i^*w|^2=w^*h_i h_i^*w\ge\eta_i,
\quad i=1,\ldots,m.
\]
Thus one quadratic transmit-power objective is constrained by generally nonconvex quadratic coverage inequalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Find the least-power common beamformer whose received quadratic signal power meets every multicast user’s threshold.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The multicast beamforming problem is a complex QCQP with constraints \(w^*h_i h_i^*w\ge\eta_i\).

source_refs.locator: 3.9 The GOP for Quadratically Constrained Problems p. 96

source_witnesses.locator: 3.9 The GOP for Quadratically Constrained Problems p. 96

children.title: Detection QCQP Interface
children.top_down_role: QCQP model structures arising in signal or symbol detection.

knowledge_statements.title: Detection QCQP Interface
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Maximum-likelihood BPSK detection represented as a binary equality-constrained QCQP.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For the real observation model \(y=Hs+\varepsilon\), suppose \(s\in\{-1,1\}^n\) and \(\varepsilon\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^2I_p)\) with \(\sigma^2>0\). Maximum-likelihood BPSK detection solves
\[
\widehat{s}\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{s\in\mathbb{R}^n}\|y-Hs\|_2^2
\quad\text{subject to}\quad
s_i^2=1,
\quad i=1,\ldots,n.
\]
The objective expands as
\[
s^{\mathsf T}H^{\mathsf T}Hs-2y^{\mathsf T}Hs+y^{\mathsf T}y,
\]
so the detector is a nonconvex QCQP whose quadratic equalities encode the BPSK constellation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under zero-mean isotropic Gaussian noise, maximum-likelihood BPSK detection minimizes the quadratic observation residual while sign equations restrict every transmitted symbol to plus or minus one.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\widehat{s}\) is an optimal solution of the displayed binary QCQP.

children.title: Shared Relaxation Interface
children.top_down_role: Common lifted-relaxation and recovery connections across multicast and detection models.

knowledge_statements.title: Shared Relaxation Interface
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Common semidefinite lifting for multicast and binary-detection QCQPs, including affine quadratic terms through augmentation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let real-valued Hermitian quadratic functions be
\[
q_i(z)=z^*A_i z+2\operatorname{Re}(a_i^*z)+\alpha_i,
\quad i=0,\ldots,m,
\]
where \(z\in\mathbb{C}^n\), \(A_i\in\mathbb{H}^n\), \(a_i\in\mathbb{C}^n\), and \(\alpha_i\in\mathbb{R}\). Define \(\widetilde z=(z^{\mathsf T},1)^{\mathsf T}\),
\[
H_i=\begin{bmatrix}A_i&a_i\\a_i^*&\alpha_i\end{bmatrix},
\qquad Z=\widetilde z\widetilde z^*.
\]
Then \(q_i(z)=\operatorname{tr}(H_iZ)\), while \(Z\succeq0\), \(\operatorname{rank}(Z)=1\), and \(Z_{n+1,n+1}=1\). Dropping the rank constraint gives the semidefinite relaxation
\[
\min_{Z\in\mathbb{H}^{n+1}}\operatorname{tr}(H_0Z)
\quad\text{subject to}\quad
\operatorname{tr}(H_iZ)\mathrel{\bowtie_i}b_i,
\quad i=1,\ldots,m,
\qquad Z\succeq0,
\qquad Z_{n+1,n+1}=1,
\]
where each \(\bowtie_i\) is one of \(\le\), \(\ge\), or \(=\). Homogeneous multicast permits the unaugmented specialization \(W=ww^*\). Real BPSK detection uses the real symmetric version of the augmented lift and includes \(Z_{ii}=1\) for \(i=1,\ldots,n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Multicast and binary detection both admit semidefinite lifting; augmentation by a fixed final coordinate is required when the quadratic model contains linear or constant terms.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Removing \(\operatorname{rank}(Z)=1\) produces a semidefinite relaxation containing every lifted feasible QCQP point.

knowledge_statements.title: AC Optimal Power Flow QCQP Interface
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Rectangular-voltage AC optimal power flow with explicit generation and branch-flow variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(v\in\mathbb{R}^{2N}\) collect rectangular bus voltages. For suitable symmetric network matrices \(Y_k,\overline{Y}_k,M_k,Y_{ij},\overline{Y}_{ij}\), an AC-OPF QCQP minimizes a quadratic generation cost \(f(p^g)\) subject to
\[
p_k^g-p_k^d=v^{\mathsf T}Y_kv,
\quad q_k^g-q_k^d=v^{\mathsf T}\overline{Y}_kv,
\quad \underline{V}_k^2\le v^{\mathsf T}M_kv\le\overline{V}_k^2,
\]
\[
P_{ij}=v^{\mathsf T}Y_{ij}v,
\quad Q_{ij}=v^{\mathsf T}\overline{Y}_{ij}v,
\quad P_{ij}^2+Q_{ij}^2\le(S_{ij}^{\max})^2,
\]
together with linear bounds on generation. All displayed equalities and inequalities are quadratic in the joint variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Rectangular voltages make AC power balances and voltage limits quadratic; explicit branch-flow variables retain quadratic thermal limits, producing a QCQP.
assumptions_latex: The network admittances and demands are fixed.
Generation cost \(f\) is quadratic and generation bounds are linear.
Branch apparent-power limits are modeled using explicit real and reactive flow variables.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The stated rectangular-coordinate AC-OPF model is a QCQP in \((v,p^g,q^g,P,Q)\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Common quadratic Lyapunov condition for a continuous-time uncertain linear system.

source_refs.locator: 9.2 Robust Stability Analysis p. 297

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The family \(\dot x=A(\delta)x\), \(\delta\in\Delta\), is quadratically stable if there exist \(P\in\mathbb{S}^n\) and \(\alpha>0\) such that \[P\succ0,\qquad A(\delta)^{\mathsf T}P+PA(\delta)\preceq-\alpha I_n\quad\text{for every }\delta\in\Delta.\] Equivalently, the single quadratic function \(V(x)=x^{\mathsf T}Px\) decreases uniformly along every member of the uncertain system family. When the uncertainty and decrease requirements admit quadratic descriptions in a common lifted variable, this universally quantified condition can be passed to an S-procedure certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Quadratic stability requires one positive-definite quadratic Lyapunov function whose derivative is uniformly negative for every admissible uncertainty.

knowledge_statements.title: S-Procedure Interface
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional inhomogeneous S-procedure using scalar nonnegative multipliers.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(d,m\in\mathbb{N}\), let \(z\in\mathbb{R}^d\), and let \(q_i(z)=[z;1]^{\mathsf T}Q_i[z;1]\) with \(Q_i\in\mathbb{S}^{d+1}\) for \(i=0,1,\ldots,m\). If there exist multipliers \(\lambda_i\geq0\) satisfying \[Q_0-\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_iQ_i\succeq0,\] then \(q_0(z)-\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_iq_i(z)\geq0\) for every \(z\in\mathbb{R}^d\). Consequently, every \(z\in\mathbb{R}^d\) satisfying \(q_i(z)\geq0\) for all \(i=1,\ldots,m\) also satisfies \(q_0(z)\geq0\). Thus the displayed semidefinite feasibility condition is a directly verifiable certificate for the quadratic implication.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Nonnegative scalar multipliers certify a quadratic implication when their weighted matrix difference is positive semidefinite.
assumptions_latex: Each quadratic has the representation \(q_i(z)=[z;1]^{\mathsf T}Q_i[z;1]\) with \(Q_i\in\mathbb{S}^{d+1}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The matrix inequality \(Q_0-\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_iQ_i\succeq0\) certifies \(q_i(z)\geq0\ \forall i\in\{1,\ldots,m\}\Rightarrow q_0(z)\geq0\).

children.title: Certificate Conservatism Boundary
children.top_down_role: Structural regimes where the certificate interface becomes conservative or inconclusive.

assumptions_latex: The quadratic functions are finite-valued on \(\mathbb{R}^d\).
In the one-premise case, there exists \(\bar z\) with \(q_1(\bar z)>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For one strictly feasible premise the scalar certificate is exact; without the qualifying hypotheses, it is only sufficient.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exactness boundary between the lossless one-premise S-lemma and general multi-premise S-procedure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(m=1\), strict feasibility \(q_1(\bar z)>0\) makes the implication \[q_1(z)\geq0\ \Longrightarrow\ q_0(z)\geq0\] equivalent to the existence of \(\lambda_1\geq0\) such that \(q_0(z)-\lambda_1q_1(z)\geq0\) for every \(z\in\mathbb{R}^d\). This is the lossless S-lemma boundary. If strict feasibility is removed, exactness can fail: the premises \(z\geq0\) and \(-z\geq0\) imply \(-z^2\geq0\), but no nonnegative multipliers make \(-z^2-\lambda_1z+\lambda_2z\) globally nonnegative. With multiple quadratic premises, scalar-multiplier feasibility is generally sufficient rather than necessary unless additional structure restores exactness.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The S-procedure is exact for one strictly feasible quadratic premise, but can become conservative without regularity or with multiple premises.
knowledge_statements.title: Certificate Conservatism Boundary

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The lossless one-premise S-lemma and the general conservatism boundary are nontrivial claims with no cited source. The displayed counterexample concerns multiple premises and therefore does not by itself establish failure caused solely by removing strict feasibility in the one-premise case.

assumptions_latex: The uncertainty set is \(\mathcal U=\{u\in\mathbb{R}^d:q_i(u)\geq0,\ i=1,\ldots,m\}\).
For fixed \(x\), both \(-f(x,\cdot)\) and every \(q_i\) are quadratic in \(u\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The robust constraint follows from the semidefinite certificate \(Q_0(x)-\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_iQ_i\succeq0\), \(\lambda_i\geq0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: S-procedure representation of a robust scalar constraint with quadratic uncertainty dependence.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Write \(-f(x,u)=[u;1]^{\mathsf T}Q_0(x)[u;1]\) and \(q_i(u)=[u;1]^{\mathsf T}Q_i[u;1]\). The robust quadratic constraint \[f(x,u)\leq0\quad\text{for every }u\in\mathcal U\] is the quadratic implication \(q_i(u)\geq0\) for all \(i\) implies \(-f(x,u)\geq0\). A sufficient finite-dimensional representation is the existence of \(\lambda_i\geq0\) such that \[Q_0(x)-\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_iQ_i\succeq0.\] If \(Q_0(x)\) is affine in \(x\), this certificate is a linear matrix inequality in \((x,\lambda)\); exactness depends on the applicable S-lemma conditions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A universally quantified quadratic constraint becomes a quadratic implication and admits a sufficient semidefinite certificate through nonnegative multipliers.
